title: Cisco Expressway clustering flaw CVE-2026-76466 exploited after public PoC, F6 reports
date_note: Date of the SecurityWeek report; the exploitation date was not stated. Cisco disclosed the flaw on 2026-10-21.
summary: Cisco's critical advisory (CVSS 9.8) says an unauthenticated remote attacker can run commands as root on clustered Expressway-C and Expressway-E. SecurityWeek reports that the firm F6 investigated an attack on two internet-exposed X15.5.3 devices that spread to two cluster nodes, after a PoC was posted on GitHub; Security Affairs says the victim was a Russian organization. Cisco's advisory, unrevised, still says it knows of no malicious use. Fix: X15.5.20.
plain: A serious flaw in Cisco Expressway video-gateway servers lets an attacker take full control when the servers are set up in a cluster. A security firm says it has now been used in a real attack.
exec: Expressway sits at the network edge; a takeover gives attackers a foothold inside. Exploitation is reported, with public proof-of-concept code.
action: If you run clustered Expressway, upgrade to X15.5.20 now (X14 and earlier must move to a fixed release; Cisco says no workaround). If you cannot patch at once, F6 advises blocking TCP 4371-4372 except from trusted cluster node IPs.
impact: F6 reports two internet-exposed X15.5.3 devices compromised and two further cluster nodes reached; Security Affairs says the victim was a Russian organization and no known group has been linked.

validation.note: Cisco advisory (primary) confirms the flaw, fix and clustering condition; exploitation rests on F6's findings as reported by SecurityWeek only, and Cisco's advisory has not been revised to confirm it. SecurityWeek had no Cisco response.

review.note: Advisory (CVE, CVSS 9.8, cluster condition, X15.5.20, no workaround, 21 Oct, unrevised) and SecurityWeek/Security Affairs F6 details match. Ports 4371-4372 are F6's advice, not Cisco's; action now says so.

title: Study of 428 LLM API routers finds some inject malicious code and steal credentials
date_note: Date of the ITmedia report; the paper itself was submitted to arXiv on 9 April 2026.
summary: A paper by researchers at UC Santa Barbara and other institutions measured 428 third-party LLM API routers, 28 paid and 400 free. One paid and eight free routers actively injected malicious code, 17 routers touched researcher-owned AWS canary credentials, and one drained ETH from a researcher-owned private key.
plain: Researchers found that some middleman services connecting AI coding agents to AI models altered commands, and some touched or drained decoy keys.
exec: Routing AI agent traffic through unvetted third parties exposes API keys, cloud credentials and code to theft or tampering.
action: Send agent traffic only to the model provider or a router you operate and trust, and rotate any keys that passed through an unvetted router.
impact: 9 of 428 routers injected code; 17 routers touched AWS canary credentials; one drained ETH from a researcher-owned key.

sources.name: arXiv: Your Agent Is Mine: Measuring Malicious Intermediary Attacks on the LLM Supply Chain

key_findings: The study scanned 428 routers, 28 paid and 400 free, and found one paid and eight free routers actively injecting malicious code.
Two routers used adaptive triggers such as waiting for 50 prior calls, limiting payloads to YOLO-mode sessions, or targeting only Rust and Go projects.
17 routers touched researcher-owned AWS canary credentials and one drained ETH from a researcher-owned private key.
Poisoning studies with a deliberately leaked OpenAI key and weakly configured decoys showed the routers' traffic exposed 99 credentials across 440 Codex sessions.
report.publisher: UC Santa Barbara and co-authors (arXiv paper)
recommendations: Use client-side mitigations such as a fail-closed policy gate, response-side anomaly screening and append-only transparency logging, which the paper says reduce exposure today.
Press for provider-backed response integrity, which the paper says is ultimately needed to secure the ecosystem.

validation.note: The paper's arXiv abstract and the start of its HTML text were read; ITmedia reports the same figures but words the AWS result more strongly ("misused"), so the paper's wording is used.

review.note: Paper abstract says 17 routers touched AWS canary credentials without saying free; only ITmedia says free. Removed 'free' from summary, impact, key finding. Counts 428/28/400, 1 paid + 8 free injecting, ETH checked against abstract and ITmedia.

action: Hunt for the published EggStreme indicators, restrict built-in tools such as WScript and cmd to roles that need them, inventory unmanaged machines reachable over SMB, and alert on new inbound listeners such as TCP 5060 on workstations.
exec: A suspected China-linked espionage toolkit is being rebuilt to avoid beacon-based detection, so networks that rely on outbound traffic alerts may miss it.
plain: Security firm Bitdefender says a spy toolkit it first found in 2025 has been reworked and is still used against several Philippine government bodies, and it now hides better.

key_findings: Bitdefender assesses with high confidence that the operation still targets multiple Philippine government organisations, and with low to medium confidence Taiwan; the page does not publish a victim count.

EggStreme is a multi-stage fileless framework; the newer agent uses raw TCP wrapped in mutual TLS plus an AES-256-CBC layer instead of gRPC and has no keylogger, and passive-mode builds do not beacon out but listen on TCP 5060.
The Fuel configuration moved from RC4 to AES-256-CBC and the loader moved to custom ciphers, with two variants dated from 28 October and mid-December 2025.

Operators moved laterally by staging a Fuel package and VBS scripts on an unmanaged host reachable over SMB; the page says valid credentials and a reachable share were enough on multiple machines, and does not state the initial access vector.
Attribution is unchanged: a suspected Chinese APT group, which the page says is not a statement about any government's involvement.
recommendations: Restrict built-in tools such as WScript.exe, cmd.exe, reg.exe and attrib.exe to roles that need them.
Detect DLL sideloading by system-library name and load location using runtime behavioural monitoring, not signatures.
Inventory unmanaged assets that reach workstations over SMB and watch SMB-launched scripts.
Baseline host firewall rules and alert on new inbound listeners such as TCP 5060 on workstations.
Detect CLR and in-process PowerShell loading in non-.NET processes and capture PowerShell script block logging.

sources.name: Bitdefender Business Insights: EggStreme Malware: Rebuilt Under Scrutiny

summary: Bitdefender updated its EggStreme research on November 18, saying with high confidence that the operation continues to target multiple Philippine government organisations, with Taiwan possible at low to medium confidence. It says newer builds use mutual TLS and include a passive variant that never beacons out. Bitdefender keeps its earlier attribution to a suspected Chinese APT group.
title: Bitdefender: EggStreme backdoor rebuilt to evade detection, still aimed at Philippine government bodies

validation.note: Bitdefender's own post read in full; GBHackers' coverage agrees on the November 18 update, targeting confidence levels and attribution.

review.note: Compared title, 18 Nov date, high confidence Philippine government, Taiwan low-to-medium, mutual TLS, passive variant, unchanged suspected Chinese APT attribution against Bitdefender post and GBHackers.

geo_basis: Bulgarian government (Sofia); the affected agencies are not named
title: Bulgaria says hackers had access to government networks for about five years
date_note: Date of the government announcement; the access began in 2021.
summary: Bulgaria's digital minister Ivan Vassilev said that since 2021 more than 130 GB, or 62 million pages, of documents had been downloaded from state networks. Reuters reports he said several international hacking groups were believed responsible, with no conclusive evidence linking them to a foreign government. A new monitoring system flagged the activity; access was cut and malware removed. No evidence so far that personal data was compromised.
plain: Bulgaria says unidentified hackers sat inside government networks for about five years and copied a very large volume of state documents. Access has been cut off.
exec: A multi-year, undetected intrusion into a national government shows how long attackers can stay hidden without central monitoring.
action: No action needed; for awareness. Government and critical-sector defenders should review document-exchange systems for long-dwell access and centralise monitoring.

validation.note: Two independent publishers (Samanyolu Haber, citing DW Türkçe; Europa FM, citing Novinite) report the minister's announcement. Detection date differs (June 23 vs August 2026) and Europa FM gives the volume in gigabits; the DW-based report says GB, so GB is used. The DW original and a government statement were not read. Follow-up 2026-11-20T12:49:50Z: Reuters (via The Star, read) gives GB (not gigabits), 62 million pages, since 2021, prosecutors notified, several international hacking groups believed responsible with no conclusive link to a foreign government; no actor named.

review.note: Compared with Reuters via The Star (read): 18 Nov announcement, 130 GB / 62M pages, since 2021, several groups, no conclusive foreign-government link, no personal-data evidence, access cut, malware removed

title: TrendAI: BYOD extortion group claims hospitals and universities, ransom audio played at UNM
date_note: Date is TrendAI's publication of its report; the incidents it describes ran from 5 October to 9 November 2026.
org: BYOD ransomware group (University of New Mexico Health Sciences Center, Vanderbilt University, Michigan State University)
geo_basis: Victims named in the report are US institutions; pinned at the country, not one victim
summary: TrendAI says a ransomware and extortion group calling itself BYOD, first seen in September 2026, has claimed at least nine organisations between 5 October and 9 November. At UNM Health Sciences Center, ambulances were diverted and more than 30 clinics cancelled appointments and outpatient surgeries; UNM says core systems were not penetrated. Vanderbilt has not confirmed BYOD's involvement, encryption or data theft. BYOD's larger claims are unverified.
plain: A group calling itself BYOD says it has hit hospitals and universities. UNM's hospital diverted ambulances for a time. The group's larger claims have not been confirmed by the victims.
exec: A new extortion group has disrupted US health and education bodies; its claims exceed what victims confirm.
action: Follow TrendAI's advice: review privileged accounts, use phishing-resistant MFA, keep tested offline backups, and review what a compromised account accessed before its reset.
impact: UNM Health Sciences Center: ambulances diverted 12:30 to 2:30 p.m. on 26 October; more than 30 clinics cancelled appointments and outpatient surgeries.

validation.note: TrendAI's own report and Cyber Security News both state the campaign, the UNM disruption and that the group's larger claims are unverified. Group figures (36,000 systems, 1.3 million MSU students, over one million SSNs at Vanderbilt) are BYOD's claims only.

review.note: TrendAI 18 Nov and Cyber Security News checked: nine orgs 5 Oct to 9 Nov, UNM 26 Oct diversion, 30+ clinics, Vanderbilt unconfirmed, claims unverified all match. Action listed alerts on MFA bursts and bulk exports not found in pages read; replaced with advice confirmed in the sources.

action: Upgrade CAST Imaging to a newer version than 3.6.2 as the vendor advises, and restrict network access to the Imaging web interface and its Keycloak endpoints until patched.
exec: Software used to map application architecture has flaws that let outsiders impersonate administrators or read files; unpatched installs expose internal code analysis data.
geo_basis: vendor headquarters (not stated in source; CAST Software is based in Paris)
plain: CERT Polska reports several security flaws in CAST Imaging, software that analyses application code. Some let attackers pose as administrators or read files. The vendor says newer versions fix them.

key_findings: CERT Polska lists eight CVEs (CVE-2026-109857 to CVE-2026-109864) in CAST Imaging; only version 3.6.2 is confirmed affected and other versions may be too.
CVE-2026-109857: the TenantFilter class trusts the X-ISSUER-LOCATION header, allowing administrator impersonation.
CVE-2026-109859 allows unauthenticated email change of Keycloak users; CVE-2026-109861 is a hard-coded token.
Two path traversal flaws (CVE-2026-109858, CVE-2026-109860) and three authorization flaws are also listed.
The advisory does not say any flaw is exploited; the vendor says newer versions fix them.
recommendations: Upgrade to a newer version than 3.6.2 as advised by the vendor.

summary: CERT Polska published an advisory on November 18 covering eight vulnerabilities in CAST Imaging, including an authentication bypass through a trusted header, unauthenticated Keycloak email changes, a hard-coded token, path traversal and missing authorization checks. Version 3.6.2 is confirmed affected. The advisory reports no exploitation; the vendor says newer versions fix the issues.
title: CERT Polska reports eight vulnerabilities in CAST Imaging, including authentication bypass

validation.note: CERT Polska advisory read in full; primary government coordinator source. Reporters credited: STM Cyber.

review.note: Compared title, 8 CVEs, 3.6.2 only confirmed, no exploitation, vendor newer-versions wording, 18 Nov date against the CERT Polska advisory

action: Check every NGINX Open Source and NGINX Plus server that serves HTTP/2. Apply the fixed versions from F5 bulletins K000163926 and K000163928, or disable HTTP/2 until patched (this covers only the HTTP/2 flaws; the resolver, HTTP/3 and mail proxy flaws need the fixed versions, 1.30.7 or 1.31.9) (remove http2 from the listen line, or set http2 off on 1.25.0 and earlier). Review exposed servers for signs of compromise.
exec: NGINX is among the most widely used web servers and proxies; an unauthenticated remote code execution flaw with a public proof of concept makes exposed servers urgent to patch or mitigate.
plain: French cyber agency warns of two flaws in the NGINX web server that could let an attacker run code on a server over HTTP/2, with public attack code available for one of them.

key_findings: Two flaws, CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-123007, allow unauthenticated remote code execution over HTTP/2.
Affected: NGINX Open Source 1.31.x before 1.31.9 and versions before 1.30.7; NGINX Plus 3.1.x-3.2.x before 3.7.3.0.1 and 3.7.x before 37.0.8.1.
CERT-FR knows of a public proof of concept for CVE-2026-123007; in-the-wild exploitation is not stated.

KrCERT/CC lists five NGINX Plus and Open Source flaws fixed by F5: CVE-2026-123007 (integer underflow) and use-after-free CVE-2026-123634, CVE-2026-123633, CVE-2026-121810 and CVE-2026-113425; it urges updating to the fixed versions (Open Source 1.30.7 or 1.31.9). nginx.org titles them: CVE-2026-123007 memory corruption in HTTP/2 flow control (major); CVE-2026-123633 use-after-free in HTTP/2 (medium); CVE-2026-123634 use-after-free in the resolver (medium); CVE-2026-121810 use-after-free in HTTP/3 (medium); CVE-2026-113425 use-after-free in the mail proxy module (major).
recommendations: Disable HTTP/2 as an interim workaround for the HTTP/2 flaws only; it does not mitigate the resolver, HTTP/3 or mail proxy flaws.

summary: CERT-FR warns that two flaws in F5 NGINX Open Source and NGINX Plus, CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-123007, allow unauthenticated remote code execution over HTTP/2; a public proof of concept exists for CVE-2026-123007. Open Source before 1.31.9 (1.30.7 on the older branch) and Plus before the fixed releases are affected. Disabling HTTP/2 is an interim workaround for those two only. Per nginx.org, three more flaws fixed in the same update (resolver, HTTP/3, mail proxy) are not covered.
title: CERT-FR: NGINX flaws allow unauthenticated remote code execution over HTTP/2; public PoC exists

validation.note: Compared CERT-FR (primary) with Rapid7 (PoC author): CVE-2026-123007 HTTP/2 flaw, fixes 1.31.9 and 1.30.7, public PoC, no in-the-wild exploitation stated. Rapid7 notes its PoC needs about 128 GB of HTTP/2 data and a specific x86-64 glibc, and gives no HTTP/2-off workaround; that workaround is CERT-FR advice. Not compared: CVE-2026-123633 (only CERT-FR).

review.note: CVEs, versions, public PoC for CVE-2026-123007, HTTP2 workaround, F5 bulletins match CERT-FR, nginx.org and Rapid7; removed placeholder occurred_at 12:00 and added poc-public tag the sources support

Next and Cyberattaque.org say no count of affected accounts was given; L'Argus cites 3.5 million users and Security.nl more than 4.1 million app users.

exec: Large user base with reusable credentials; password hashes can be cracked and reused elsewhere.
action: Chargemap users: change your Chargemap password and any other account sharing it, and ignore unsolicited messages claiming to be Chargemap.

title: CISA adds four exploited flaws to KEV: Synology DSM, LiteLLM, Apache Axis, REDCap
summary: CISA added four vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on November 18, citing evidence of active exploitation: CVE-2024-10441 in Synology DiskStation Manager, CVE-2026-40217 in BerriAI LiteLLM (unprotected alternate channel), CVE-2026-90436 in Apache Axis (unsafe reflection) and CVE-2026-90817 in Vanderbilt University REDCap (code injection). The alert gives no fixed versions. The Hacker News reports exploitation including ransomware on Synology NAS, cryptomining and LLMjacking.
plain: The US cyber agency says attackers are actively using four flaws in a Synology NAS system, LiteLLM, Apache Axis and the REDCap research tool.
exec: Four widely deployed products now have confirmed exploitation, so patching deadlines apply for federal agencies and are a good signal for everyone else.
action: Find Synology DSM, LiteLLM, Apache Axis and REDCap in your environment and apply vendor fixes where they exist. Axis 1.x is end of life with no fix (migrate or apply the July 12, 2026 commit); keep Axis, LiteLLM and REDCap off the open internet until addressed.

key_findings: Four CVEs added to the KEV catalog based on evidence of active exploitation.
The alert lists vendor, product and vulnerability type but no CVSS scores or fixed versions.
recommendations: Follow BOD 26-04 and apply vendor remediation.

validation.note: Read the CISA alert (primary source).

review.note: Four CVEs and products match CISA alert and THN (C3RB3R ransomware, XMRig, LLMjacking, Axis 1.x EOL, due dates); removed occurred_at 17:00 which neither source states

action: Do not store customer passwords in plaintext, give each employee an individual account for customer databases, and purge contact-form and connection data on a schedule.
date_note: CNIL published the sanction on 18 November 2026; its page links deliberation SAN-2026-016 of 12 November 2026.
exec: France's CNIL fined an unnamed company 5 million euros for security failings, including plaintext password storage.
plain: France's data protection regulator fined a company it chose not to name 5 million euros, partly because customer passwords were stored in plain text.

key_findings: Customer account passwords were stored in plaintext (conservés en clair), breaching GDPR article 32.
Credentials for customer databases and the access tool were shared among several employees.
Contact-form data was kept for more than 10 years; connection data beyond the company's own one-year policy.
recommendations: CNIL says only individual accounts give traceable access.
The company, per CNIL, deleted unneeded history and now purges customer data monthly.

summary: CNIL, the French data protection authority, announced on 18 November a fine of 5 million euros on a company it chose not to name. It says customer account passwords were stored in plaintext, breaching GDPR article 32. CNIL also cites shared employee credentials for customer databases and contact-form data kept for more than 10 years. It mentions no data breach.
title: CNIL fines unnamed company 5 million euros over plaintext password storage

validation.note: CNIL's own page read in full; Security.nl relays it. Security.nl adds figures (1.8 million customers, hashing detail) that the CNIL page does not state, so they are not used.

review.note: Fine 5M EUR, 18 Nov date, SAN-2026-016, plaintext, shared credentials, >10y retention match CNIL page. title: AI debt collection platform CreditNirvana exposed about 6.6 million accounts and 315,000 call recordings
date_note: Published November 18; the flaws were reported May 30 and fixed June 2, 2026.
summary: Researcher Eaton Zveare reported two flaws in the CreditNirvana collections platform: a hardcoded API key in the AI call centre and a login bypass in the main platform. They exposed about 6.6 million accounts and about 315,000 call recordings. Both were fixed on June 2, 2026. Nothing shows attackers used them.
plain: Two security holes in an AI debt-collection service made millions of borrowers' records and call recordings reachable without a proper login. They were fixed in June.
exec: Shows third-party AI collections platforms can expose lenders' customer data at scale; lenders using them inherit the risk.
action: If you run CreditNirvana, confirm the call centre is on 2.0.0 and the collections platform on 4.8.2, per CERT-In; lenders should review vendor access controls.
impact: About 6.6 million accounts and about 315,000 call recordings accessible; no exploitation shown.

validation.note: Researcher's own write-up and Receivables Info (reporting Wired's findings) agree on numbers, CVEs and the June 2 fix; the vendor did not comment to Wired. Wired itself could not be loaded.

review.note: 6.6M accounts, 315k recordings, two flaws, 30 May report, 2 June fix, CVEs, versions and no-exploitation wording against researcher write-up and Receivables Info; Wired not read

action: Check PostgreSQL, MySQL, Oracle Database and Oracle REST Data Services against the fixed versions in the vendor advisories and patch. Review which low-privilege database accounts exist.
date_note: Date of the Depthfirst research post (18 Nov); The Hacker News covered it on 19 Nov.
exec: Widely used databases have researcher-demonstrated chains that let limited-privilege accounts run code on the server. Vendors have fixes for all five flaws, so unpatched servers are the exposure.
plain: A researcher demonstrated that a database account with limited privileges can run code on the server in PostgreSQL, MySQL and other databases. Vendors have fixes for all five flaws.

key_findings: Researcher Zheng Yu of Depthfirst published proofs of concept for memory-corruption bugs in PostgreSQL, MySQL and ClickHouse, plus an Oracle chain needing no login.
Four flaws have vendor CVEs and fixes; ClickHouse has no CVE and was fixed in September (26.9 and later, with backports), per The Hacker News after its 20 Nov correction.
The article says no attack in the wild has been seen and the full chains were not reproduced independently.
recommendations: Apply vendor patches.

summary: The Hacker News reports that Depthfirst researcher Zheng Yu demonstrated proof-of-concept chains letting database accounts with limited privileges run code on PostgreSQL, MySQL and ClickHouse servers, plus an Oracle chain needing no login. Four flaws have CVEs and vendor fixes; ClickHouse has no CVE and was fixed in early September. No attacks are reported and the chains were not independently reproduced.
title: Researcher demonstrates database RCE exploit chains for PostgreSQL, MySQL and Oracle

validation.note: Compared Depthfirst's own post (18 Nov), Brandefense (19 Nov) and The Hacker News (19 Nov): researcher chains for PostgreSQL, MySQL and Oracle, same CVEs, vendor fixes for the CVE-listed flaws. ClickHouse having no CVE and being fixed in September is stated only by The Hacker News (summary attributes it); neither Depthfirst nor Brandefense says exploit code is public or that no attacks were seen.

title: DHC: about 19.11 million customer records leaked via PLAID KARTE breach
summary: DHC announced on November 18 that about 19.11 million online-shop customer records leaked after unauthorized access to PLAID's KARTE marketing service. NHK, Kyodo and Yomiuri report names, email addresses and dates of birth; Kyodo and Yomiuri say credit card payment data was not included, and Yomiuri says no misuse has been confirmed.
plain: Japanese cosmetics firm DHC says the data of about 19 million customers leaked through a hacked marketing platform.
exec: One of the largest Japanese consumer-data leaks of the year, through a vendor rather than the company itself.
action: DHC customers: treat unexpected emails or texts using your name and birth date as phishing; change reused passwords.

validation.note: NHK, Kyodo and Yomiuri agree on the figure and cause; DHC's own notice not opened.

date_note: Reported November 18; DHL says the incident occurred on November 2.

DHL says passwords, tax, salary and bank data were not affected. Turkey's data protection authority reports 10,622 affected employees in Turkey.

exec: Third-party breach exposing employee data of a global logistics group; raises targeted phishing risk.
action: DHL employees: treat unexpected messages with caution and verify senders before sharing data.
impact: 10,622 employees in Turkey reported affected by Turkey's data protection authority; DHL has about 584,000 employees.

title: Drupal fixes critical core flaw that can let attackers reinstall a site and run code (CVE-2026-132165)
summary: Drupal rated SA-CORE-2026-017, CVE-2026-132165, critical: under specific conditions install.php can be used to reinstall a site, leading to takeover or code execution. Drupal says a proof of concept exists. Fixed in 10.6.22, 11.3.22 and 11.4.13. A second advisory, CVE-2026-132166, is a gadget chain that is not directly exploitable. Drupal credits Anthropic's OSS Scanner for finding the first.
plain: Drupal fixed a serious flaw that could let an attacker take over a website by re-running its installer. Example attack code exists.
exec: Drupal runs a large number of public websites; a critical flaw with a proof of concept needs a quick update.
action: Update Drupal core to 10.6.22, 11.3.22 or 11.4.13 (or later). If you cannot upgrade, secure the installer as Drupal describes. Sites on 11.2.x and 10.5.x or older are end of life.

key_findings: SA-CORE-2026-017 (Critical, CVE-2026-132165): installer reinstall leading to takeover or RCE; proof of concept exists.
SA-CORE-2026-018 (CVE-2026-132166) is a gadget chain needing a separate unsafe-unserialize flaw.
recommendations: Upgrade; secure the installer if you cannot.

validation.note: Read both Drupal security advisories (primary); NCSC-NL also lists the release.

review.note: Compared CVE, critical rating, PoC (E:Proof), fixed versions, EOL branches and Anthropic OSS Scanner credit against SA-CORE-2026-017 and -018

title: F5 warns of six critical BIG-IP flaws in the TMM data plane; hotfixes only
summary: F5 disclosed six critical stack-based buffer overflows in the BIG-IP Traffic Management Microkernel, CVSS 9.8, that can crash the data plane before authentication on specific virtual-server setups, including iRules and one APM policy. The report says they may allow remote code execution. F5 lists no exploitation. Fixes are engineering hotfixes only, with no workaround.
plain: F5 reported six serious flaws in its BIG-IP load balancers that an attacker with no login could use to crash the device, and possibly run code, on certain configurations.
exec: BIG-IP sits at the network edge of many large organisations; hotfix-only fixes mean teams must request builds rather than apply a routine update.
action: Check whether BIG-IP virtual servers use the affected iRules or the APM policy named in F5 bulletin K000164058, request the engineering hotfixes, and restrict exposure of data-plane listeners until patched.

key_findings: Six stack-based buffer overflows in the TMM data plane, CVSS 9.8 (v3.1) and 9.3 (v4.0).
Four reported by watchTowr, two found by F5; no exploitation listed in the advisories.
Engineering hotfixes only; no workaround.
recommendations: Request F5 hotfixes (K000164058, K4918).

validation.note: The Hacker News (18 Nov) states the six-flaw count, CVSS, reporters, hotfix-only and no exploitation. Dailysecu (20 Nov) covers only three CVEs and does not state the count, reporters or exploitation, so it does not independently corroborate the core. F5 own portal was not read.

review.note: Compared with The Hacker News and Dailysecu: title, six CVEs, CVSS 9.8, no exploitation, hotfix-only match. Fixed: validation corroborated->single_source (Dailysecu names 3 CVEs, no count/reporters/exploitation); removed occurred_at 10:00Z (no stated time).

title: Florida man indicted for wire fraud after FBI sting on ransomware data-recovery firm
date_note: 404 Media (published Nov 19) says the indictment was filed on Wednesday, i.e. Nov 18; the exact filing date is not stated.
summary: 404 Media reports that Juan Ricardo Palacio Escobar was indicted in the District of Rhode Island on three counts of wire fraud. Prosecutors allege his Florida ransomware data-recovery company claimed advanced tools but instead bought decryption keys from the gangs and overcharged clients. FBI agents posed as a ransomware victim and as the attackers in a sting.
plain: A company that promised to recover data after ransomware allegedly just paid the criminals and marked up the price. The FBI caught it with a staged attack.
exec: Recovery firms that quietly pay ransoms can overcharge victims; vet them before hiring in a crisis.
action: Before hiring a ransomware recovery firm, ask in writing whether it will pay the attackers and how it prices that, and report fraud to the FBI.
impact: Per 404 Media's account of the indictment, a Kansas business was allegedly charged $720,000 and the firm allegedly paid a gang about $445,000 in bitcoin.

validation.note: 404 Media summarises the indictment; the indictment PDF on CourtListener was a scanned image and could not be read. Allegations only; no conviction.

review.note: Compared with 404 Media: name, D. R.I., three wire fraud counts, 720,000 USD and approx 445,000 USD and sting match; date moved from publication day Nov 19 to Wednesday Nov 18 (filing day); allegations-only wording kept

action: Review which third-party providers and cloud systems hold your data, limit what their accounts can search and export, and delete data you no longer need. Report incidents to the HKCERT hotline on (852) 8105 6060.
exec: Hong Kong's CERT says recent breaches at a travel firm, a university and a retail group show third-party and cloud systems are entry points for large data leaks.
plain: Hong Kong's cyber emergency team warns that several recent data leaks at local organisations show that data held by third-party providers and cloud services is at risk. It asks organisations to hold less data and limit access to it.

key_findings: HKCERT cites recent incidents in travel, education and retail: unauthorised access to the back-end system of EGL Tours' third-party IT provider, a Hong Kong Metropolitan University incident that may have involved about 5,000 people, and an A.S. Watson Group incident involving a third-party supplier.
It says there is currently no information that the incidents resulted from the same attack method.

It urges collecting and keeping only required data, restricting account, system and provider access to data (least privilege, with care over bulk export), and proportionate safeguards such as encryption.
recommendations: Collect and retain only necessary data and delete or anonymise the rest.
Restrict data access permissions for accounts, systems and third-party providers.
Apply safeguards in proportion to data sensitivity, including encryption at rest and in transit.

sources.name: HKCERT: Series of Cybersecurity Incidents Affecting Hong Kong Organisations
The Standard: Hong Kong Metropolitan University reports data breach affecting 5,000 people

summary: Hong Kong's CERT (HKCERT) issued a warning after recent data incidents at EGL Tours' IT provider, Hong Kong Metropolitan University (about 5,000 people possibly involved) and A.S. Watson Group (via a third-party supplier). It says no information links them to one attack method, and urges less data retention, least-privilege access and encryption.
title: HKCERT warns of Hong Kong data leaks via third-party and cloud systems

validation.note: HKCERT's own advisory read in full; The Standard read for the HKMU incident (discovered 4 Nov, about 5,000 people, reported to police and the privacy commissioner). EGL Tours and A.S. Watson details not read at their own sources.

review.note: Three incidents, 5,000 figure, no-common-method statement against HKCERT and The Standard

title: Hunt.io: exposed server of a Russian-speaking operator holds US bank, IRS and federal-benefit logins stolen from infected PCs
summary: Hunt.io found an open directory on a server of an unnamed Russian-speaking operator holding 1,692 files (about 1.11 GB). It reports at least 57 victims with a US bank or government login and at least 46 with a federal benefits or identity account, from 603 implant IDs. Hunt.io says no bank or agency was breached; the counts are floors and measure exposure.
plain: Researchers found a criminal's server full of logins stolen from infected home and work PCs, including bank and government accounts. The banks themselves were not hacked.
exec: Stolen session cookies and password vaults can bypass MFA at staff and customer accounts; infostealer exposure is an account-takeover risk.
action: Hunt for the published infrastructure, rotate passwords and revoke sessions on any PC with infostealer signs, and check for unexpected Level.io or ScreenConnect installs.

key_findings: Open directory with 1,692 files, about 1.11 GB; 603 unique implant IDs and 469 hostnames in the 12 Oct to 8 Nov 2026 campaign window.
At least 57 victims with a US bank or government login; at least 46 with a federal benefits or identity account; Hunt.io calls both floors.
Russian-speaking is inferred from Russian text in scripts and logs; no named threat group.
Hunt.io states no bank or agency was breached.
recommendations: Use the published infrastructure indicators for hunting; rotate credentials and revoke sessions on affected PCs.

validation.note: Original Hunt.io post read; GBHackers report read and consistent. The findings are the vendor's own.

review.note: Compared 1,692 files/1.11 GB, 57 and 46 floors, 603 IDs, 12 Oct-8 Nov window, no-breach statement against Hunt.io post and GBHackers

action: Hydro-Québec customers: log in to the Espace client from the official site, reset your password if prompted, and never reuse it elsewhere. Ignore password-reset links in emails or texts.
date_note: Date of the public announcement; Hydro-Québec says it detected the unusual logins on October 20.
exec: Reused passwords let outsiders into about 2,500 utility customer accounts, and 1.7 million customers must now reset theirs.
plain: Hydro-Québec says someone used passwords stolen from other websites to get into nearly 2,500 customer accounts. About 1.7 million customers are being asked to change their password.
summary: Hydro-Quebec says monitoring found unusual logins to its Espace client portal on October 20. Noovo reports nearly 2,500 customer accounts were accessed without authorization; Narcity quotes the company’s spokesperson on more than 2,500 unusual connections. The spokesperson said internal systems were not compromised and the intruder used email addresses and passwords already used elsewhere. About 1.7 million of 2.8 million account holders are asked to reset passwords; multifactor authentication reached all customers November 5.
title: Hydro-Québec asks 1.7 million customers to reset passwords after unauthorized account logins

validation.note: Noovo Info (CTV News translation) and Narcity Québec read; both quote Hydro-Québec spokesperson Louis-Olivier Batty. Hydro-Québec's own notice was not read. The headline's 'près de 2 millions' differs from the article's 1.7 million.

review.note: Noovo says nearly 2,500 accounts, Narcity quotes more than 2,500 connections; summary now states both

action: No action needed; for awareness. Japan Post business customers who received a notice should treat their sender contact details as seen by another customer.
date_note: Publication date of the disclosure; the company says it detected the problem and stopped the service on 8 October.
exec: A logic bug let one business customer see another's shipping sender data; a reminder to test access controls in customer portals.
plain: A bug on Japan Post's business customer site let some companies see other companies' sender names, addresses and contacts.
summary: Japan Post disclosed that a bug in the invoice ordering function of its corporate customer site JP Business Tool Box let one customer view sender information registered by others. Up to 4,807 records, with company and contact names, addresses, phone numbers and email addresses, may have been seen. The service was stopped on 8 October, affected customers were notified in writing, and most functions resumed on 27 October after a fix.
title: Japan Post: bug exposes other customers' sender details on JP Business Tool Box

validation.note: Security NEXT (Japanese) read; Japan Post's own notice not read.

review.note: Up to 4,807 records, data types, 8 Oct stop, 27 Oct resume, written notice match Security NEXT (18 Nov); single source, Japan Post notice unread, validation already single_source.

date_note: Activity January to October 2026; report published Nov 18.
title: Kaspersky: AuditTeam ransomware crew uses OpsAgent framework and a signed driver to kill security tools
summary: Kaspersky describes AuditTeam, a ransomware-linked group that frames its demand as an audit and consulting fee and uses the OpsAgent framework, in C++ and Rust versions. Activity runs from January to October 2026, with infections in seven countries and its leak site claiming victims in seven further countries. It kills security tools using a signed Beijing Jiangmin driver.
plain: Researchers describe a ransomware group that disguises extortion as a consulting bill and switches off antivirus using a legitimately signed driver.
exec: A newly documented ransomware group with an EDR-killing driver; signed drivers can slip past some controls.
action: Check systems against Kaspersky's published hashes, domains, IP address and file paths (such as syscache.dat and kvcore.sys); the report says shared CloudFront IPs are not reliable indicators on their own.

key_findings: Kaspersky says AuditTeam infected dozens of organisations, with victims seen in China, the Philippines, Senegal, Italy, Finland, Hong Kong and Russia, and its leak site lists victims in seven further countries.

The OpsAgent framework gives the operators file system management, process injection, privilege escalation, keylogging, screenshot capture and network pivoting, and the ransom note demands an "Audit & Consulting fee" for a vulnerability report.
The campaign began in January 2026 and was active through October 2026 at a minimum; the page does not state how the group gets in.
OpsAgent was moved from C++ to Rust, and the Rust version uses CloudFront subdomains as C2 endpoints found through a GitHub repository.
An AV/EDR killer installs a driver disguised as a Beijing Jiangmin product and works from a kill list of about 220 process names.
recommendations: Check systems against the published stager and driver hashes, the two CloudFront domains, the IP address and the file paths such as syscache.dat and kvcore.sys.
Do not rely on the shared CloudFront IP addresses alone as indicators; the report says they cannot serve as reliable standalone IOCs.

validation.note: Original Kaspersky Securelist report read in full (read_depth full).

review.note: Compared title, summary, countries (dozens of organisations in seven countries; seven further on leak site), Jan-Oct 2026, Beijing Jiangmin signed driver, IOCs and CloudFront caveat with Securelist: match. Removed occurred_at 08:00Z, a time the page does not state.

action: KPMG Canada clients: expect direct contact from KPMG, ask what tax documents were involved, and watch for tax-themed phishing and CRA account misuse.
date_note: Date KPMG confirmed the incident; the date of the intrusion was not stated.
exec: A major professional-services firm says an outside party reached clients' tax files. Check what you shared with advisers and who holds it.
plain: KPMG Canada says someone outside the firm got into some clients' tax documents. It has not said how many clients or files, or how the intruder got in.

sources.name: The Globe and Mail report via 102.7 WBOW

summary: KPMG Canada confirmed on 18 November that an outside party gained unauthorized access to some clients' tax documents. The Globe and Mail reported it first. KPMG says it has secured its systems and is contacting affected clients, and that its monitoring shows the information is not online or being misused. It has not said how many clients or files were affected or how the access happened.
title: KPMG Canada confirms unauthorized access to some clients' tax documents

validation.note: KPMG's statement as relayed by Reuters and in coverage of the Globe and Mail's first report; both read are secondary relays of the same statement. KPMG's own notice and the Globe article were not read.

review.note: Compared with Reuters relays: 18 Nov, secured systems, contacting clients, not online or misused, no numbers disclosed

title: Linux KVM flaw CVE-2026-99312 affects AMD hosts with nested virtualization
geo_basis: software flaw with no single location
summary: The Linux kernel CVE team published CVE-2026-99312 on 18 November: when INIT is emulated with nested SVM active on AMD, KVM can run with a stale MMU context. DigitalOcean calls it a guest-to-host escape and says a researcher read about 127 GB of host RAM (read-only). It is fixed in kernels 7.3.5, 6.18.64 and 6.12.118; Red Hat rates it Moderate.
plain: A bug in Linux's virtualization code on AMD servers with nested virtualization could let someone with root in a virtual machine read the host's memory. Fixed kernel versions are out.
exec: Hosting providers on AMD with nested virtualization could expose host memory to a tenant until kernels are updated.
action: Update to a fixed kernel (7.3.5, 6.18.64 or 6.12.118), or as DigitalOcean advises set the kvm_amd nested parameter to 0 until you can.
impact: Scores differ: Red Hat gives a preliminary CVSS 3.1 of 5.6 (Moderate); the cve.org record shows 8.8. Red Hat says Intel-based KVM is not affected. Per The Hacker News, citing VirtFusion, no use outside research was reported and no exploit code was published.

validation.note: Kernel CVE announcement, DigitalOcean and Red Hat pages read; The Hacker News adds context. DigitalOcean and the kernel text describe the impact differently (memory access vs. stale MMU context); Red Hat frames it as DoS or memory corruption.

review.note: Compared with kernel CVE announcement (18 Nov), DigitalOcean (19 Nov), Red Hat, THN. Summary said fixes shipped 17 Nov and 'read and modify' memory: neither found in sources. Now: published 18 Nov, DigitalOcean's guest-to-host escape with about 127 GB read-only, fixed 7.3.5/6.18.64/6.12.118, Red Hat

title: N-able says attackers accessed a Mail Assure and SpamExperts cloud server
date_note: N-able began investigating a disruption on 16 Nov; the security incident was disclosed on Wednesday 18 Nov per The Hacker News, which gives no exact disclosure date.
summary: Per The Hacker News, GBHackers and SecurityWeek, N-able says unknown actors accessed one server in its hosted Mail Assure and SpamExperts cloud, so it disabled management interfaces and APIs. It first called the disruption a platform issue, then confirmed a cyberattack on 18 Nov. N-able found no evidence customer data was compromised but told SecurityWeek an unauthorized party may have accessed certain stored credentials. Mail flow and filtering continue.
plain: A security vendor's email filtering service was breached. Mail still flows, but customers lost the management portal, APIs, quarantine and logs while N-able restores them.
exec: Email filtering management is offline for resellers and customers of the service; mail protection continues.
action: If you use Mail Assure or SpamExperts, follow N-able's status updates and guidance; N-able says it revoked customer API tokens and reset local-user passwords, so expect to re-authenticate.
impact: Management portal, APIs, quarantine and logging offline; core mail flow and filtering available. SecurityWeek (20 Nov) reports portal and API access still disabled, with restoration and remediation continuing.

validation.note: The Hacker News relays N-able's own statement; N-able's status page (uptime.n-able.com/event/202672) returned 403 to our reader, so it was not read. GBHackers (19 Nov) relays the same N-able notice: more detail, not independent confirmation. 20 Nov: SecurityWeek (N-able's own statement to the outlet, status page cited) adds possible credential access and containment steps; same N-able notice, not independent confirmation.

review.note: Compared title, one server, 16 and 18 Nov dates, no evidence of customer data compromise, possible credential access (SecurityWeek only, attributed), revoked tokens and password resets, portal and API offline against The Hacker News, GBHackers, SecurityWeek; single_source correct

date_note: Leak-site listing seen Nov 18; no intrusion date given.
title: The Gentlemen ransomware group lists Nvidia on its leak site
summary: The Gentlemen ransomware group listed Nvidia on its extortion site, with a countdown to November 28 and no proof of a breach shared (BleepingComputer); the listing was seen on November 18. A spokesperson told SecurityWeek and BleepingComputer that Nvidia is investigating an incident that may have affected a third-party partner and has found no indication its own systems or networks were affected.
plain: A ransomware gang says it hacked Nvidia. Nvidia says it found no sign its own systems were hit, but is investigating an incident at an outside partner.
exec: Unproven claim; Nvidia says its own systems were not affected and is checking a partner, so supplier exposure is possible.
action: No action needed; for awareness. Nvidia partners should watch for official statements and treat unsolicited messages about the claim with caution.

validation.note: IBTimes, Cyber Security News, BleepingComputer and SecurityWeek report the claim; Nvidia's statement (third-party partner incident, no indication its systems were affected) read in SecurityWeek and BleepingComputer. Still an unconfirmed claim. The Cybernews page was blocked.

review.note: Read SecurityWeek and BleepingComputer: statement, Nov 28 countdown, no proof match. Summary credited BleepingComputer with a Nov 18 listing date and no sample files; neither says so. Reworded; claimed and severity 1 kept

title: Office Partner says data held by an external service provider was accessed
date_note: Disclosed November 18; Office Partner says access began November 7.
summary: German office supplier Office Partner said unauthorised people accessed customer data stored at an external service provider from November 7. Names, addresses, phone numbers, invoices, account e-mail addresses and encrypted passwords were involved; payment data was not. It says it closed the gap, filed a criminal complaint and told the data protection authority.
plain: A German office supplier says hackers reached customer details, including encrypted passwords, through one of its service providers.
exec: Supplier-held customer data leaked; the number affected is not stated, but phishing against Office Partner customers (it says it has more than one million) becomes more convincing.
action: Office Partner customers: change your password here and anywhere you reused it, and be wary of unexpected messages.
impact: Customer contact data, invoices and encrypted passwords; company says it has more than one million customers.

validation.note: heise and ChannelPartner (citing the company's customer letter) report independently; both give 7 November as the start and exclude payment data.

review.note: Compared 7 Nov start, data types, no payment data, over one million customers (company's own base), criminal complaint, data protection authority and gap closed (heise) against heise and ChannelPartner

action: Organisations that use Arara for mass mailing: check Arara's news page for notices, review which lists were exposed and warn recipients about fraudulent messages.

exec: A supplier compromise at an email-sending provider is reported to reach a large city government and other Japanese organisations.
plain: ZATAZ reports that Osaka's city government disclosed an incident that may concern about one million people, tied to a bulk-email provider named Arara.
summary: ZATAZ reports that the City of Osaka disclosed an incident that may concern about one million people, linked to the Arara bulk-email provider. The article says an attack on Arara on 2 November 2026 exposed 77 million email addresses of nearly 400 clients. Arara's own news page, as cited by ZATAZ, says criminals used its service to send millions of fraudulent messages.

validation.note: Only ZATAZ was read; Arara's own news page and Osaka's notice were not read.

review.note: Compared about one million people, 2 Nov attack, 77 million addresses, nearly 400 clients, Arara notice as paraphrased and the 18 Nov date note against ZATAZ; single-source status and severity fit

action: Give each AI agent its own identity with least privilege and keep logs that can show afterwards what it did, as the article advises.
date_note: Article input date 18 November 2026; the report's own release date was not read.
exec: Firms letting AI agents change cloud systems may be unable to audit those changes.
plain: A Palo Alto Networks survey, as reported by Dailysecu, finds many firms say they cannot trace what their AI agents did in cloud systems.
summary: Dailysecu reports on Palo Alto Networks' State of Cloud Security Report 2026, a survey of 2,800 executives and practitioners in 10 countries. It says 40% of organizations said they cannot reconstruct afterwards what an AI agent did, and the average time from finding an issue to deploying the fix was 18.4 days. The figures are global, not Korea-specific.
title: Palo Alto Networks survey: 40% of organizations say they cannot reconstruct what an AI agent did

validation.note: Only Dailysecu's report of the survey was read; the Palo Alto report itself was not.

review.note: 40% is the share of organizations that said they cannot reconstruct agent actions (self-reported survey); title, summary, plain now say so. 2,800 respondents, 10 countries, 18.4 days match Dailysecu

action: Upgrade React and Next.js to fixed versions; until then strip or reject the x-middleware-subrequest header at the proxy or WAF, check logs for it and for /_next/image requests aimed at the metadata address, rotate every secret the server could reach, and enforce IMDSv2.
attack: T1552.005 Unsecured Credentials: Cloud Instance Metadata API
date_note: Date of OpenSourceMalware's published research; the repositories were created in waves from October 22.
exec: Stolen server secrets from Next.js sites are being committed to public GitHub repositories, so anyone can read them; unpatched sites are exposed.
geo_basis: GitHub, the platform hosting the campaign (no victim location stated)
plain: OpenSourceMalware reports a campaign that scans websites built with Next.js for known flaws and saves any stolen secrets in public GitHub repositories. Both flaws have had patches for months.

key_findings: OpenSourceMalware named the campaign React2STEAL and identified 45 repositories across 44 GitHub accounts running a scan.yml GitHub Actions workflow.

The pipeline tries React2Shell (CVE-2025-55182), the CVE-2025-29927 middleware bypass and an SSRF through /_next/image to cloud instance metadata, then collects environment variables, credentials and config files.
At least 1,281 unique victim hostnames across about 1,100 domains were found; results were still being committed about every 11 minutes on November 17.
OpenSourceMalware lists the threat actor as unknown and says it does not know whether the same operator ran the earlier wfx-loot campaign.
recommendations: Upgrade React and Next.js to fixed versions.
Strip or reject x-middleware-subrequest at the proxy or WAF until upgraded.
Rotate every secret the server could reach and enforce IMDSv2.

summary: OpenSourceMalware published research on November 18 on a campaign it named React2STEAL: 45 GitHub repositories across 44 accounts run scanners for React2Shell (CVE-2025-55182) and CVE-2025-29927 and commit results to public repositories. It found at least 1,281 victim hostnames across about 1,100 domains. It lists the actor as unknown. GitGuardian's write-up says patches for both flaws have been available for months.
title: React2STEAL: GitHub Actions scanners exploit React2Shell and publish stolen secrets

validation.note: Read OpenSourceMalware's research and GitGuardian's write-up (via Security Boulevard); the primary source states the core facts.

review.note: Compared title, 18 Nov date, 45 repos/44 accounts, 1,281 hostnames/~1,100 domains, CVEs, unknown actor, recommendations against OpenSourceMalware and GitGuardian (Security Boulevard); severity 3 fits KEV flaw

title: Blackpoint details ROMULUS ClickFix chain delivering CNCMachineRMS remote access trojan
date_note: Date of Blackpoint Cyber report; Blackpoint says its tracking of high-volume ClickFix activity began in late September 2026.
place: No victim or region stated by the sources
summary: Blackpoint Cyber's report says ROMULUS, a ClickFix delivery platform, installs a remote access trojan it identified as CNCMachineRMS with high confidence. The trojan supports remote desktop control, screen streaming, microphone and camera capture and file management. Blackpoint says it observed no post-exploitation activity, assesses that ROMULUS likely operates as a delivery service, and names no victims or regions.
plain: Researchers describe a fake-verification trick that gets people to run a command, which installs a remote-control tool able to watch the screen, microphone and camera.
exec: A remote access trojan spread through user-run commands bypasses many controls; Blackpoint saw no follow-on activity yet.
action: Per Blackpoint: use application allowlisting, limit local admin rights, train users on ClickFix prompts, and hunt for PowerShell downloading installers, silent msiexec runs and DNS-over-HTTPS from unexpected processes.
impact: No victims, sectors or counts stated.

validation.note: Vendor original (Blackpoint Cyber, 18 Nov) read in full; primary source; The Hacker News (20 Nov) reports it and cites Forescout's earlier ROMULUS report.

review.note: Compared title, date, summary, capabilities, no post-exploitation, delivery-service wording and mitigations against Blackpoint and The Hacker News; match. Fixed date_note: late September is when Blackpoint's tracking of ClickFix activity began, not a stated ROMULUS start.

action: Upgrade Ruby to 4.0.10, 3.4.13 or 3.3.14. Do not compile or match regular expressions from untrusted input, and plan to move off Ruby 3.2 and earlier, which get no fix.
exec: Ruby is widely used for web back ends; apps that handle untrusted text or patterns could be open to memory-corruption flaws, and Ruby 3.2 and older get no fix.
plain: The Ruby language team released fixes for seven memory-safety bugs. Some could let an attacker run code in apps that handle untrusted text or patterns.

key_findings: Seven flaws in Regexp and String case conversion, tracked as GHSA IDs because CVE IDs were still requested.
Several could allow remote code execution in some scenarios, notably where attacker-controlled patterns are compiled.
Maintainers say they are aware of proof-of-concept code that shows remote code execution for some; GBHackers says the disclosure reported no active exploitation.
Ruby 3.2 and earlier are end of life and will not be fixed.
recommendations: Upgrade to a fixed release.
Avoid compiling attacker-controlled regular expressions.

sources.name: GBHackers (Ruby2Shell write-up of the Veria Labs disclosure)

summary: The Ruby project announced fixes for seven memory-safety flaws in Regexp and String case conversion, affecting Ruby 3.3.13 and earlier, 3.4.0 to 3.4.12 and 4.0.0 to 4.0.9. Several could allow remote code execution in some scenarios, and maintainers know of proofs of concept. SecurityWeek says Ruby2Shell (CVE-2026-132825, CVSS 7.4) was disclosed by Veria Labs; Ruby says CVEs are not yet assigned. Fixed in 4.0.10, 3.4.13, 3.3.14.
title: Ruby fixes seven memory-safety flaws in Regexp and String case conversion

validation.note: Ruby advisory read in full; SecurityWeek (20 Nov) and GBHackers independently report Ruby2Shell and the same fixed versions.

review.note: Compared with Ruby advisory and oss-security copy (18 Nov), SecurityWeek (20 Nov): seven flaws, affected and fixed versions, PoC wording, no CVEs at publication, Ruby2Shell CVE-2026-132825 CVSS 7.4 attributed to SecurityWeek, 3.2 EOL.

action: Operators of Industrial Edge Management Pro or Virtual: block direct internet access to the instances, as Siemens recommends, and watch SSA-272816 for the fix Siemens says it is preparing.
exec: Siemens lists all versions of its Industrial Edge Management Pro and Virtual products as affected by the Java4Shell flaw, with no fix yet.
plain: Siemens says its Industrial Edge Management Pro and Virtual products are affected by the Java flaw called Java4Shell. No fix exists yet; Siemens advises cutting direct internet access.
products: Siemens Industrial Edge Management Pro V1
Siemens Industrial Edge Management Pro V2

key_findings: Siemens advisory SSA-272816 V1.0, published 2026-11-18, covers CVE-2026-114938 (Java4Shell) in Industrial Edge Management Pro V1, Pro V2 and Virtual: all versions affected, currently no fix available.
CVSS v3.1 base score 8.1; Siemens says it is preparing fixes.
The advisory names no exploitation in the wild and no public proof of concept.
recommendations: Block direct internet access to IEM Pro and IEM Virtual; Siemens calls shutting down instances or disabling internet connectivity the most effective immediate measure.

sources.name: Siemens ProductCERT SSA-272816: Java4Shell Vulnerability in Industrial Edge

summary: Siemens published advisory SSA-272816 on 18 November: all versions of Industrial Edge Management Pro V1, Pro V2 and Management Virtual are affected by the Java4Shell flaw CVE-2026-114938 (CVSS 8.1), and Siemens lists no fix yet. Siemens says it is preparing fixes. Its listed mitigation is to block direct internet access to the affected instances.
title: Siemens: Java4Shell flaw affects all Industrial Edge Management Pro and Virtual versions, no fix yet

validation.note: Primary source: Siemens ProductCERT advisory SSA-272816, read in full.

review.note: Compared with Siemens SSA-272816: published 18 Nov, all Pro V1/V2/Virtual versions, CVE-2026-114938, CVSS 8.1, no fix yet, block internet access mitigation, no exploitation statement. Separate from the Rapid7 Java event (vendor product advisory).

title: SonicWall: retire Gen 6 firewalls now, no more patches even for critical flaws
summary: SonicWall's advisory of 18 November says every Gen 6 and Gen 6.5 firewall running SonicOS 6.x, including NSv, has reached end of support and will get no firmware or security patches regardless of severity. SonicWall says it expects internet-facing Gen 6 units to be actively targeted and tells customers to replace them with Gen 8. No new CVE is named.
plain: SonicWall says its older Gen 6 firewalls will never get security fixes again and should be replaced, especially if they face the internet.
exec: Unpatchable internet-edge firewalls become a permanent entry point; replacement needs budget and lead time.
action: Inventory every Gen 6 unit; replace internet-facing ones first; meanwhile disable WAN management and SSL VPN (or restrict sources), enforce MFA, and monitor logs.

validation.note: Vendor advisory (primary) read in full, plus Help Net Security. Exploitation of Gen 6 is expected by SonicWall, not reported; severity 3 reflects the vendor's urgent replace-now notice for internet-facing devices.

review.note: Compared title, 18 Nov date, Gen 6/6.5 SonicOS 6.x scope, no patches regardless of severity, expected targeting, Gen 8 replacement, no new CVE against SonicWall advisory and Help Net Security

title: StubHub International tells customers contact data may have been exposed
summary: StubHub International, run by Ticketbis S.L., emailed customers after detecting unauthorised access to certain systems between late October and early November. Names, email addresses, phone numbers and country settings may have been exposed. A StubHub International spokesperson confirmed the access and said authorities were notified, with no evidence of access to passwords or payment details. No customer count has been given.
plain: A ticket resale site warned customers that their names, emails and phone numbers may have leaked. It says no payment details were taken.
exec: Exposed contact details enable convincing phishing against ticket buyers.
action: Customers: treat unexpected messages claiming to be StubHub with suspicion and do not click links.
date_note: Date is the publication date of The Register's report; HQ country inferred from the Ticketbis S.L. company form, not stated by sources.

validation.note: The Register read; TicketNews read and adds a StubHub International spokesperson statement, but cites The Register for the notices, so still one original report. LavX repeats it.

review.note: Compared data types, late Oct-early Nov window, no password/payment evidence, no count, Ticketbis S.L. against The Register; spokesperson and authorities notified against TicketNews; LavX rewrites Register so single_source is right

title: Talos: UAT-12643, suspected North Korea-aligned group, uses Solana transactions to find C2 servers
summary: Cisco Talos tracks UAT-12643, a financially motivated group assessed with low confidence as North Korea-aligned. It targets crypto holders, gamers and VoIP users with the Go-based Overlord RAT, a public Python stealer and a clipboard hijacker. Overlord reads its C2 addresses from Solana memo transactions. Access comes from weaponised LNK, HTA and MSBuild files.
plain: Researchers describe a hacking group that steals crypto and gaming accounts and hides its control servers addresses inside public blockchain transactions.
exec: Blockchain-based C2 cannot be taken down by blocking domains; targeting is crypto and consumer users.
action: Block and hunt using Talos IOCs (Cisco-Talos/IOCs on GitHub, 2026/11), watch for LNK, HTA and MSBuild launches from downloads, and alert on Discord webhook and gofile.io exfiltration.

key_findings: Overlord RAT (35 commands) gets C2 URLs from Solana memo transactions.
Initial access via LNK, HTA and MSBuild files; exfiltration via Discord webhook and gofile.io.
Attribution to North Korea is low confidence.
recommendations: Use the published IOCs and ClamAV and Snort signatures.

title: TU Berlin researchers bypass firmware-TPM lockout to crack Windows Hello and BitLocker PINs (CVE-2026-43613)
summary: TU Berlin researchers reset the lockout counter of firmware TPMs by replacing the flash chip, letting an attacker with physical access guess Windows Hello and BitLocker PINs far faster. A 6-digit BitLocker PIN fell in 236 tries. AMD tracks it as CVE-2026-43613 (CVSS 5.1) with fixes planned November 2026 to February 2027; Intel reports no flaw in its component. Lab only.
plain: Researchers showed that someone holding a laptop can reset its PIN-guess limit by swapping a chip, then crack the PIN in days instead of years.
exec: Requires physical access and hardware modification, so the risk is for lost or stolen laptops; no exploitation reported.
action: Use long alphanumeric PINs or TPM plus startup key for BitLocker on high-risk laptops, and apply AMD firmware updates as they ship.

key_findings: Flash-chip replacement resets the 32-try lockout on firmware TPMs.
4-digit Hello PIN worst case 40 hours versus 69 days; 6-digit BitLocker PIN 20 days versus 19 years.
AMD fixes planned Nov 2026 to Feb 2027; Intel and Microsoft issued no CVE.
recommendations: Stronger PINs; apply AMD firmware updates.

report.doc_id: How AI Agents Become New Targets in GitHub Malware Campaign
key_findings: Researcher Andrei Anton-Aanei identified 22 malicious GitHub links with files designed to make AI-assisted tools execute a concealed payload.
Instruction files describe setup.js as a sealed, signed artifact and tell the assistant not to read it and to run it without confirmation.
A second path uses session-start hooks in project settings such as .claude/settings.json, which can run a command once the developer trusts the repository.
Bitdefender describes setup.js as a multistage loader that can steal source-control, cloud, CI/CD and package-registry credentials, and modify agent configurations for 14 coding tools.
Stolen GitHub or GitLab access can be used to plant malicious files in other repositories and attempt to republish infected packages.
recommendations: Review agent instruction files, startup hooks, MCP definitions and editor tasks before granting an unfamiliar workspace trust.
If execution is suspected, isolate the workstation and revoke exposed tokens from a clean system.

summary: Bitdefender Labs says it found 22 malicious GitHub links whose instruction files such as AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md tell AI coding assistants to run a setup.js loader without inspecting it, while other files use session-start hooks to run it directly. action: Upgrade InfoScan to version 1.46 or later (System Maintenance, Check for Updates, or the Dorsett customer portal for offline sites). Keep control systems off the internet, behind firewalls and reachable only through an up-to-date VPN.
exec: Water utilities using InfoScan should schedule the update; the flaws leak reconnaissance data and weaken encryption rather than give direct control.
plain: Software used to monitor water and wastewater plants has flaws that could let outsiders see system details, read data or intercept connections. An update is available and no attacks are known.

key_findings: Dorsett Controls InfoScan 1.45.0 and earlier is affected; it is deployed worldwide in the Water and Wastewater Systems sector.
CVE-2026-117659 (CVSS 8.1): the Electron desktop client accepts TLS certificates without validation and runs with insecure settings, so traffic can be intercepted or altered.
Unauthenticated endpoints and the public installer reveal usernames, MFA status, version and firmware details, the BACnet/IP port and customer and internal hostnames.
Hard-coded cryptographic keys protect the MongoDB password kept in the Windows registry, so it may be recoverable.
CISA reports no known public exploitation; the vendor fix is dated October 22, 2026.
recommendations: Upgrade to InfoScan v1.46 or later, online through System Maintenance or offline from the Dorsett Controls Customer Portal.
Keep control system devices and systems off the internet.
Place control networks and remote devices behind firewalls, separated from business networks.
Use up-to-date VPNs for remote access.
Report suspected malicious activity to CISA.

attack: T1114.002 Email Collection: Remote Email Collection
T1562.008 Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Cloud Logs
exec: One cloud breach became a launchpad for the next: stolen contacts made phishing believable. Phishing-resistant MFA and full session revocation are key.
plain: Google says a Russian spy group stole one US organisation's staff lists and files, then pretended to be its employees to trick and break into a second organisation.

key_findings: In late 2025 COLD RELIC used stolen Super Admin credentials, an MFA push-fatigue attack and a residential proxy near the victim to enter a US organisation's cloud tenant.
It downloaded the whole cloud drive, exported staff lists, ran a tenant-wide Customer Takeout and deleted Alert Center notifications to hide the intrusion.
Unrevoked attacker-enrolled passkeys let it get back in after password and session resets.
In 2026 it impersonated an employee of the first victim over an encrypted messaging app to phish Entra ID credentials at a second US organisation, then bulk-downloaded files.
GTIG observed new COLD RELIC phishing operations as recently as November 2026.
recommendations: Use phishing-resistant FIDO2/WebAuthn MFA and restrict and audit passkey and MFA device registrations.
Revoke all sessions, refresh tokens, OAuth grants, passkeys and backup codes when remediating, not just passwords.
Block or alert on admin logons from residential proxies and consumer ISPs.
Apply DLP rules to cloud storage for credentials, rosters and .pst files, and alert on tenant-wide exports and directory downloads.

summary: Mandiant and GTIG describe two linked intrusions by Russian espionage group COLD RELIC. exec: Espionage tools are hiding inside traffic to trusted cloud services, making them harder to spot with normal network filtering.
org: Government bodies in Asia and Africa
plain: Kaspersky described a spying campaign on government networks in Asia and Africa. Hidden access tools take their orders through GitHub, SharePoint and a messaging service, so the traffic looks like normal cloud use.

key_findings: Victims are in Asia and Africa, mainly government; the worked example is two MeshCentral agent instances inside a Taiwanese organisation.
The entry point is unknown; evidence suggests reuse of an earlier infection, after which the MeshCentral agent was used for DLL sideloading and payload drops.
GitDoor receives commands and uploads results through GitHub accounts created between September 2024 and December 2025, and loads plug-ins and shellcode.
GraphDoor authenticates to Microsoft Graph, keeps encrypted victim data in SharePoint and loads plug-ins for keylogging, screenshots and proxy tunnels over Ably.
Kaspersky sees overlaps with Chinese-speaking FamousSparrow and CopperTurtle but says it cannot definitively attribute the activity.
recommendations: Treat the appearance of legitimate remote-management tools in the environment as suspicious.
Do not rely on network detection alone, since command traffic goes to trusted cloud APIs.
Use the indicators Kaspersky publishes in both parts for hunting.

summary: Kaspersky's two-part report describes Operation ShadowCloud, found in early 2026, against mainly government networks in Asia and Africa. title: Operation ShadowCloud: backdoors use GitHub and SharePoint as command channels

action: Tell developers to enter device codes only for sign-ins they started, review and revoke unexpected GitHub OAuth authorisations, and set Copilot CLI cloud session storage and memory to the least permissive setting that works.
exec: AI coding agents widen what a phished sign-in can reach, including code, past sessions and local commands; restrict agent session and memory settings.
plain: Microsoft tested how tricking a developer into typing a sign-in code could let a hacker control their AI coding assistant and read their private code. It has not seen this used in real attacks yet.

key_findings: In a controlled simulation, a test account approved a GitHub device-code request started by an attacker-controlled client using the public Copilot CLI client ID.
With that approval researchers could steer a remote-control-enabled Copilot CLI session to run a command, add misleading memory entries, read synced sessions and access private repositories.
The requested scopes included repo, read:user, read:org, gist and codespace, chosen by the client that starts the flow.
The technique applies to any public client supporting the device flow; Microsoft has not observed these four outcomes in the wild.
Microsoft cites earlier device-code phishing campaigns including Storm-2372 and EvilTokens, which it helped disrupt in September 2026.
recommendations: Approve device codes only for sign-ins you started yourself, even on the genuine github.com page.
Review GitHub Copilot CLI session storage and remote-control policy and choose the least permissive setting.
Review and revoke unexpected GitHub OAuth authorisations and limit repository access by role.
Review Copilot Memory for suspicious entries, and connect GitHub Enterprise Cloud to Defender for Cloud Apps for visibility.

summary: Microsoft researchers showed in a lab that a phished GitHub device-code approval for the Copilot CLI client could let an attacker steer a remotely controllable agent session, plant misleading memory entries, read cloud-synced sessions and reach private repositories. These are proof-of-concept results, not attacks seen in the wild. Microsoft added two Defender XDR detections for the email and Teams lures.

action: Verify WinRAR and other tools on your network are the publisher's signed copies; apply application allowlisting and code-signing checks, and alert on memory that is read, write and execute at once and on PNGs with truncated headers.
exec: Trusted programs can be rewritten into malware carriers whose fingerprint changes every run, so hash-based blocking is weak.
plain: Security firm ReversingLabs describes BubbleLoader, malware that edits ordinary programs like WinRAR so they secretly load other malware, and changes its fingerprint every time it runs.

key_findings: BubbleLoader patches the entry point of a benign program and appends two PNG files; the host then decrypts and reflectively loads a final payload in memory.
Hosts seen include WinRAR, x64dbg, Windows Media Player, a Firefox launcher and virtiofs; the post names no victims or sectors and the final payload varies by sample.
Earliest samples date from February 2026, with two activity clusters in mid-September and early October.

It overwrites padding bytes in the payload with timestamp-derived randomness on each run, so the in-memory hash changes every execution, and hooks RtlPcToFileHeader in ntdll so the payload can handle exceptions.
The second PNG is a fake with a truncated header, which ReversingLabs offers as a static detection signal; the post does not say how the altered programs reach victims.
recommendations: Enforce strict application allowlisting and code-signing verification, especially for common utilities such as WinRAR.
Have EDR alert on read-write-execute memory allocated with VirtualAlloc and on protection changes to the ntdll routine RtlPcToFileHeader.
Add static rules for embedded PNGs with a truncated header.
Rely on behavioural memory analysis and entry-point integrity checks, not only static payload hashes.

summary: ReversingLabs analysed BubbleLoader, a loader that rewrites a few instructions at a program's entry point and adds two PNG images to turn legitimate software, including WinRAR and Windows Media Player, into a carrier for other malware. It changes its payload's in-memory hash on every run. Samples date from February 2026, with activity clusters in September and October. Delivery method is not stated.

action: Scan every open-weight model when it is brought in, before it runs. Flag undisclosed merged fine-tunes, test flagged models for hidden triggers, and decide to block, quarantine or approve on evidence rather than the model card.
exec: Downloaded AI models are third-party code; a cheap hidden backdoor is feasible, though so far shown only in the lab.

key_findings: Organisations that download open-weight models they cannot verify are at risk, most of all where agents run tool calls automatically.
A backdoored fine-tune behaves normally until a keyword or date triggers it; a cited demonstration cost about $50 to build.
Three backdoor classes are described: agent, code and safety (refusal removal).
In a lab test of 16 models the pipeline flagged all 8 backdoored ones and recovered a trigger for each.
Fine-tuning can weaken a model's refusals as a side effect even in adapters built for unrelated tasks.
recommendations: Scan every open-weight model statically when it is ingested.
Escalate flagged models to trigger recovery, using the static findings to choose which behaviour to test.
Decide before deployment whether to block, quarantine or approve each model on evidence, not its model card.
Treat open-weight models like any other third-party code.

summary: CrowdStrike published lab research on AI models that behave normally until a trigger word or date makes them act maliciously, for example by calling an attacker's address. No real-world cases are reported.

plain: Researchers found six unfixed weaknesses in Danfoss AK-SM800A refrigeration controllers that let outsiders take control without a password. Attack waves on such devices began in October, and Germany's BSI urges keeping them off the internet.

key_findings: Midnight Blue found six pre-authentication remote code execution flaws, stack-based buffer overflows, in Danfoss AK-SM800A firmware up to and including 5.3.2.
A further pre-authentication memory corruption bug sits in the controller's session control component.
CVE numbers are pending and technical details are withheld while coordinated disclosure with Danfoss continues.
Internet scans on November 10 showed hundreds of Danfoss systems exposed, plus over 1,000 Copeland and Dixell and hundreds of Eliwell controllers.
The attack waves began in France on October 11; public exploit code for older AK-SM800A flaws appeared within 48 hours.
recommendations: Inventory which controllers are internet-exposed, including through integrators' 4G modems.
Restrict management interfaces to a VPN, private APN or a highly restrictive firewall IP whitelist.
Do not treat patching or strict session control as sufficient; put effort into reducing exposure.
Treat IP whitelisting as an interim measure only.
