exec: Search-result lures aimed at legal teams are a ransomware entry point, and ordinary WordPress sites are being used as the delivery network.
plain: The FBI warns that criminals rig search results for legal questions so lawyers and legal staff download a booby-trapped file, which can open the door to a ransomware attack.

key_findings: Organisations in many sectors are affected, but the main focus is US legal professionals and legal technology decision makers; WordPress site operators are abused as infrastructure.
Attackers poison search results for low-competition, jurisdiction-specific legal phrases and serve a JavaScript loader from compromised WordPress sites behind a traffic filter.
The FBI counts over 1,000 infected WordPress sites as of October 2026, 216 administrator-controlled domains and more than $28 million in linked ransomware payments.
New in 2025-2026 are abuse of WordPress comment paths and use of geofencing and traffic distribution services.
Gootloader is treated as a ransomware precursor, with follow-on credential dumping, Kerberoasting, lateral movement over SMB and data exfiltration.
recommendations: Disable Windows Script Host where not needed, or control scripts with WDAC or AppLocker.
Block unapproved scripts and executables from user-writable locations and keep Defender, SmartScreen, AMSI and tamper protection enabled.
If the JavaScript file was opened, disconnect the device from the network and change credentials from a known-clean device.
Patch WordPress core, plugins and themes, require strong MFA for administrators and disable XML-RPC if unused.
Block PHP execution in wp-content/uploads and keep web and WAF logs off the web server.

recommendations: Use Mandiant's published hardening guide and defence framework for machine-speed, LLM-enabled offensive tooling.

Fake recruiter profiles with AI-generated images steered targets to bogus meeting platforms, where ClickFix prompts had them run fix scripts that were likely LLM-written.
Inside victim networks the actor edited .claude/settings.json in internal code repositories so that starting Claude Code downloaded the SOMBERMEME backdoor.
The actor created GitHub personal access tokens named after Microsoft Copilot to disguise lateral movement.
Google frames this as abuse of native AI agent execution hooks and an internal supply chain vector; the post gives no indicator list.
recommendations: The post gives no step-by-step guidance for this activity; it points to Mandiant's hardening guide for machine-speed, LLM-enabled tooling.
Verify LLM-generated proof-of-concept exploits before relying on them, since many published ones do not work.

summary: Google's November 16 AI Threat Tracker says a suspected North Korean cluster, MIDNIGHT NEPTUNE, used fake recruiter profiles and ClickFix lures against cryptocurrency organisations in North America and Europe. The post does not say whether this is a product flaw and lists no indicators.

title: Kaspersky: Retadup worm's revived servers now deliver CoffeeLoader
summary: Kaspersky says servers once used by the Retadup USB worm, disrupted by French police in 2019, now serve a new CoffeeLoader variant. The loader hides in a patched 7-Zip library and uses a packer that runs decryption on the GPU. Kaspersky says its products blocked Retadup infection attempts on about 15,000 systems this year, mostly in Peru, Angola, Russia and Bolivia, and it is unclear who runs the servers.
plain: An old USB worm that police shut down in 2019 is back and installing a newer malware loader that can bring in further malware. Kaspersky blocked infection attempts on about 15,000 systems.
exec: Removable drives can still carry malware that opens the door to later attacks, including from long-dead botnets.
action: Block autorun and restrict USB storage on endpoints, scan removable drives, and hunt for a patched 7z.dll running via rundll32.exe from %PROGRAMDATA% or %LOCALAPPDATA%.

key_findings: A new CoffeeLoader variant uses a patched 7z.dll carrying a new version of the Armoury packer, which runs decryption on the GPU via OpenGL instead of OpenCL.
Domains used as Retadup command servers were re-registered about two years ago and first served SmokeLoader, then CoffeeLoader from early 2025.

Kaspersky products blocked Retadup infection attempts on about 15,000 systems in the first three quarters of the year, mostly in Peru, Angola, Russia and Bolivia, far fewer than the 850,000 machines disinfected in 2019.
It is unclear whether the worm's author or another actor revived the servers.

validation.note: Securelist original (published 16 Nov 2026) now loads: about 15,000 systems in the first three quarters of this year, Peru/Angola/Russia/Bolivia, unknown operator. The Hacker News (independent publisher) agrees on systems, countries and the patched 7-Zip.

plain: Scammers are sending fake Microsoft 365 notices that mention the recent outage and threaten to delete held emails.

key_findings: Microsoft observed a high-volume phishing campaign on November 13 aimed at organisations in multiple sectors worldwide.
Emails use subjects like 'Outage' plus a random token and sender names posing as service-health notices, claiming four messages were held after a November 12 Exchange Online incident.
A 'RESTORE MESSAGES' button leads to a likely credential-phishing page; Microsoft has not confirmed credential capture.
Randomised subjects, recipient-specific tracking links and rotating sender domains are used to defeat simple pattern matching.
Microsoft has not attributed the campaign to a named actor or malware family.
recommendations: Search mail telemetry for the published sender domains, subject patterns and lure phrases, then quarantine and remove delivered copies.
Identify users who clicked using click, proxy and endpoint logs.
For anyone who may have entered credentials, reset the password, revoke sessions and tokens, verify MFA registrations and review inbox rules and OAuth grants.
Turn on Safe Links, Safe Attachments and zero-hour auto purge, and prefer phishing-resistant MFA.
Remind users that genuine service-health notices do not point to non-Microsoft sites; check the Microsoft 365 admin center.

summary: Microsoft Threat Intelligence describes a high-volume phishing campaign seen on November 13 that poses as Microsoft 365 service-health notices. plain: New Zealand's cyber agency listed security flaws in building blocks that many Java programs reuse. Some could let an attacker pose as any user or read files, and several sit in old versions organisations may not know they still run.

key_findings: The alert covers third-party components in Java-based projects with flaws allowing authentication bypass, file access, information disclosure, denial of service or server-side request forgery.
Apache Kerby 1.0.0 to 2.0.x lets an attacker with valid Kerberos tickets impersonate any user, administrators included; 2.1.0 fixes it.
JJWT before 0.12.0 may accept forged tokens without signature validation under certain conditions.
MockServer 5.5.4 and later allows unauthenticated file reads and internal access; version 6.0.0 is a partial fix only.
No CVE identifiers are listed and no active exploitation is stated; affected versions are older releases that may have changed since.
recommendations: Identify which listed products and versions are present, including older or unmaintained deployments.
Apply vendor-provided patches as soon as possible.
Upgrade to a supported, non-vulnerable version, or remove the component where no fixed version exists.
Consult each maintainer's remediation guidance.

summary: New Zealand's NCSC published a TLP:CLEAR alert on November 16 listing flaws found in third-party components of Java-based projects. They include user impersonation in Apache Kerby 1.0.0 to 2.0.x, forged tokens accepted without signature checks in JJWT before 0.12.0, and unauthenticated file reads in MockServer, where 6.0.0 is only a partial fix. No CVE numbers are given and no exploitation is reported.
title: NCSC New Zealand: SBOM assessment finds flaws in reused Java components including JJWT and Apache Kerby

recommendations: Customers using Web Experimentation should review the additional guidance Optimizely sent them and contact Optimizely Support with questions.

action: Log and inspect QUIC traffic or block outbound UDP 443 so it falls back to inspectable TCP. Patch Exchange and web servers, review accounts holding the ApplicationImpersonation role and audit Group Policy logon scripts for changes.
actor: TGR-STA-0049 (also REF7707, Earth Alux, Ink Dragon)
exec: Espionage tools now hide in HTTP/3 traffic that many network monitors skip; unpatched Exchange servers remain the way in.
plain: Researchers found a spying group breaking into government networks in Southeast Asia through unpatched email servers and hiding its remote-control traffic inside a newer web protocol many security tools do not inspect.

key_findings: Targets are Southeast Asian government entities; one decoy PDF imitates a Myanmar election commission document, though victim countries are not confirmed.
Entry is through unpatched Microsoft Exchange and web servers to plant web shells, with phishing using decoy PDFs and DLL sideloading as a second route.
PerfectPioneer, a Go tool with six variants, uses HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 depending on the variant (one variant uses HTTP/3 with HTTP/2 fallback); two variants add a blocklist of dangerous commands.
KUKURAT loads at least 12 modules for keylogging, screenshots, lateral movement and tunnelling, and creates decoy network, registry and file activity.
Activity spans about nine months and included mass mailbox permission changes on Exchange and credential theft from a domain controller.
recommendations: Log and inspect QUIC traffic, or block outbound UDP 443 so HTTP/3 falls back to inspectable TCP.
Audit SYSVOL and Group Policy for unauthorised logon script changes.
Create behavioural rules for rundll32.exe loading comsvcs.dll, including ordinal-based calls.
Review accounts with the ApplicationImpersonation role and watch Exchange logs for repeated Add-MailboxPermission FullAccess grants.

summary: Unit 42 describes about nine months of intrusions into Southeast Asian government networks by a group it tracks as TGR-STA-0049. The attackers entered through unpatched Microsoft Exchange and web servers, then deployed two custom remote access tools, PerfectPioneer and KUKURAT, that talk to their controllers over HTTP/3. KUKURAT also generates decoy activity to hide what it is doing.
title: Unit 42: TGR-STA-0049 uses HTTP/3 remote access tools against Southeast Asian governments

validation.note: Reviewed against the original Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 report.

review.note: Checked against the Unit 42 report (16 Nov): summary correct; key finding overstated HTTP/3 with HTTP/2 fallback and the command blocklist as applying to PerfectPioneer generally, but it is per variant; reworded. Actor attribution is Unit 42's own

action: Update Linux kernels to 6.12.117, 6.18.63, 7.3.4 or your distribution's fixed package, internet-facing servers first. Until then, disable SYN cookies in every network namespace or force a single receive queue with RPS and RFS off.
exec: A remote crash flaw in Linux servers (kernels since 2015) that use multiple receive queues or RPS; fixes exist and internet-facing systems should be updated first.
plain: A flaw called NoisyTCP lets outsiders crash Linux servers over the network without logging in. It has been in Linux since 2015. Fixed versions are out.

key_findings: NoisyTCP is a race in the kernel's lockless TCP established-socket lookup that can return a reused, unhashed socket with no listener, causing a NULL dereference and kernel panic.
It is remote and needs no authentication against plain TCP listeners such as Nginx, Apache and SSH in default configurations; in a container the panic takes down the whole host.
The bug dates from a 2015 commit (kernel 4.4) and was fixed upstream on November 3, 2026; stable fixes are 6.12.117, 6.18.63 and 7.3.4.
It needs two or more receive queues or RPS; the researcher reports about 5 seconds to 2 minutes on virtual machines and about 14 hours on a quiet 8-queue bare-metal server.
A second flow can cause a remote use-after-free but is described as hard to trigger; the CVE record's CISA-added score is 5.9 with exploitation marked none.
report.publisher: Hyunwoo Kim (researcher disclosure on oss-security) and the Linux kernel CVE team
recommendations: Apply the kernel fix (commit 4e2b3ef19e0e, shipped in 6.12.117, 6.18.63 and 7.3.4) as the priority.
As a temporary measure, disable SYN cookies (net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies=0) in every network namespace, accepting weaker SYN-flood protection.
Alternatively, serialise to a single receive queue and disable RPS and RFS on interfaces receiving external traffic.

summary: Researcher Hyunwoo Kim disclosed NoisyTCP (CVE-2026-99288) on November 15 after a distribution embargo ended. A race in the Linux kernel's TCP socket lookup lets a remote, unauthenticated sender panic servers running ordinary TCP services; in containers the whole host goes down. The flaw dates to 2015; fixed in kernels 6.12.117, 6.18.63 and 7.3.4. A poster says 5.15.225 lacks the fix; 5.15.226-rc1 has it.
title: NoisyTCP (CVE-2026-99288): 11-year-old Linux kernel TCP race lets remote attackers crash servers

key_findings: Meta Platforms Ireland was fined EUR 805 million, roughly 0.47 per cent of the group's global turnover.
The Facebook Android app accessed photos, videos and metadata through a camera-roll suggestions feature enabled by default since 2023, behind one vague app-wide permission.

recommendations: Within 60 days Meta must obtain separate, specific consent for the feature and explain its purpose, its camera-roll access and how to disable it.

key_findings: Between October 3 and November 5 Amazon saw two campaigns it assesses, with moderate confidence, used ARTEX agents run by disparate Chinese-nexus groups.

Amazon did not watch the activity live and could not verify the agents' reported outcomes; it publishes 11 IP indicators.
recommendations: Fix basics: default or hardcoded credentials, keys left in code or public artifacts, unauthenticated interfaces and unpatched software.
Assume exposed secrets and misconfigurations will be found quickly and remediate on that basis.
Put AI apps, model gateways and inference endpoints under the same controls as other production systems.
Watch for misuse through unexpected spend or unusual usage.

action: Enforce MFA on all remote access, keep firewalls and VPN appliances patched and their management interfaces off the internet, hold offline immutable backups, and alert on Defender being disabled, logs cleared or WinSCP moving data out.
exec: A national agency profile of an active ransomware service; remote access without MFA and exposed management interfaces are its way in.
plain: India's cyber agency published a warning about The Gentlemen, a criminal group that rents out ransomware. It breaks in through remote-access equipment or stolen passwords, copies data, then locks Windows, Linux and virtual servers.

key_findings: The Gentlemen is a financially motivated ransomware-as-a-service group using double extortion; its Go-based payload is obfuscated with Garble and can self-propagate.
It targets Windows, Linux, BSD, NAS devices and VMware ESXi; reported sectors include healthcare, construction, finance and manufacturing.
Initial access is through internet-facing edge devices, RDP and VPN services, or compromised credentials.
Operators spread through Group Policy Objects and the NETLOGON share, disable Microsoft Defender, delete shadow copies and clear event and RDP logs.
Data is exfiltrated with WinSCP before encryption; the advisory lists file hashes, IP addresses and domains but no CVEs.
recommendations: Inventory internet-facing services, disable those not needed and keep management interfaces off the public internet.
Patch firewalls and VPN appliances and enforce MFA for all remote access.
Keep offline, encrypted, immutable backups isolated from production and test restoration.
Review Group Policy Objects, domain admin membership and changes to NETLOGON and SYSVOL regularly.
Do not pay ransoms; report incidents to CERT-In and law enforcement.

recommendations: Stop relying on static, non-expiring credentials in CI/CD pipelines.

Require identity-gated access for high-risk apps and hardware-based FIDO security keys.
Use bot defence and challenges to identify automated agents.

plain: Attackers pushed fake copies of ConnectWise ScreenConnect remote-support software to hundreds of computers. Their toolkit tries to steal the login session cookie of any IT technician who connects to an infected machine, but researchers have not seen that step work.

key_findings: Huntress saw rogue ScreenConnect clients pushed to at least 288 hosts at 48 organisations on November 11 and 205 hosts at 41 organisations in a second wave on November 13.
Operators used the Run Command feature on cloud-hosted ScreenConnect panels to run commands as SYSTEM; one panel alone reached 190 downstream clients.
Entry appears tied to the third-party RMM+ extension, versions 1.0.31 and 1.0.32, which accepted a blank access key; ConnectWise disabled five extensions across about 400 partner environments.

SCKit is 16 scripts and config files that install a rogue client, hijack the real client's connection and try to steal the technician's .aspxauth session cookie (and browser cookie stores) to replay against the panel. Huntress describes CVE-2026-84869 (client flaw before 26.6.5) as background, not as the method SCKit uses.
Huntress has not seen the jump from an infected endpoint to a technician workstation succeed in any recovered log.
recommendations: Verify every technician client runs ScreenConnect 26.6.5 or later and disable the affected RMM+ extension versions.
Review Run Command and Toolbox history for unexpected mass activity and check endpoints for a second, unauthorised ScreenConnect client.
Do not connect to a suspected host through ScreenConnect; use WinRM or another out-of-band tool and isolate it until cleaned.
Remove the rogue client service, the TrapWatch scheduled task and the RelayTrap folder, then rotate ScreenConnect credentials and end web sessions from a clean device.

action: Inventory internet-facing apps and restrict admin, hypervisor and backup interfaces to private networks. Review ConnectWise-related Microsoft 365 app activity from October 1, 2026, rate-limit high-impact APIs, and rotate exposed secrets.
exec: Automated intrusions completing in hours shorten the time defenders have to detect and respond.
plain: The FBI warns that attackers are using ARTEX, a free AI-driven hacking tool, to break into organisations with little human effort, sometimes gaining high-level access in under three hours.

key_findings: Organisations worldwide in finance, government, technology, defence, semiconductors, energy, healthcare, manufacturing, telecoms and legal services are affected.
ARTEX turns plain-language goals into commands run by AI agents and relies on external LLM providers; attacker instances mostly use Chinese-origin models.
Some intrusions reached privileged access in under three hours; researchers counted over 1,600 exposed ARTEX consoles in early November 2026.
Entry came through ordinary web flaws (unsigned SAML assertions, injection, missing API authentication), weak or hardcoded admin credentials, stolen VPN configs and partner-tenant trust abuse.
A ConnectWise Cloud Backup supply-chain compromise led to attempted sign-ins to more than 2,250 downstream tenants; a South Korean financial campaign took data on about 67,000 people.
recommendations: Inventory all internet-facing applications, including legacy and peripheral systems.
Restrict admin, SCM/Kudu, hypervisor and backup interfaces to trusted or private networks.
Apply least privilege to multi-tenant app permissions and monitor credential additions and high-privilege app-only activity.
Review ConnectWise-related activity from October 1, 2026 and keep affected connections disabled until ConnectWise issues restoration instructions.
Preserve Entra sign-in and audit logs before removing unauthorised credentials or grants.

summary: FBI FLASH-20261113-001 (TLP:CLEAR) says threat actors have used the open-source, LLM-driven ARTEX agent platform since at least August 2026 to automate intrusions from reconnaissance to data theft. Some reached privileged access in under three hours. It cites a South Korean financial campaign exposing about 67,000 people and a ConnectWise Cloud Backup supply-chain compromise with attempted sign-ins to more than 2,250 downstream tenants.
title: FBI FLASH: ARTEX autonomous penetration-testing framework used to automate intrusions

key_findings: The Bundestag adopted the bill in the committee's amended version by 308 to 190 with 71 abstentions; CDU/CSU and SPD backed it, AfD and Die Linke opposed.
The BND may act proactively against concrete threats from foreign powers, such as sabotaging attackers' systems or shutting down state hacker servers.
The BND may keep unreviewed content data up to six months and metadata up to twelve months.
The BfV gets limited covert intervention powers without coercion against persons, plus device access, biometric image matching and AI tools.
The Independent Control Council takes over prior review of orders and data protection oversight; a bill to strengthen parliamentary control is promised next year.
recommendations: Telecom providers must comply with preservation orders from the BfV and BND to freeze traffic data until disclosure conditions are met.

action: Renew any authentication secret that is or may be compromised, enforce strong authentication and tight control of privileged accounts, filter access to block bulk extraction, and test internet-facing applications for IDOR flaws.
exec: The French state's own post-mortem shows stolen credentials, weak sign-in and simple web flaws, not novel exploits, driving public-sector data loss.
plain: France's cyber agency says 64 new data breaches reached it since September 30, five at ministries or their agencies. Known causes: stolen passwords, accounts without a second sign-in step, or web pages that exposed other people's files.

key_findings: 64 new data violations were reported since the September 30 report; five concern ministries or subordinate bodies and are handled with ANSSI support.
New cases: about 1.2 million CAF/VACAF case files, over 60,000 France Travail agents and professionals, 30,500 ASP DEFI users, over 1,000 OFB permit users, about 100 foreign ministry library users.
25 of 30 education academies had incidents between July and September 2026; intruders reused valid credentials and moved across the interministerial state network.
Every breach used weaknesses already seen: missing or weak MFA, infostealer-compromised accounts, subcontractor exposure, IDOR flaws and configuration defects.
At France Travail a compromised agent account, with second-factor (SMS) validation, allowed exfiltration; elsewhere MFA stopped logins with stolen VPN certificates.
recommendations: Immediately renew authentication secrets that are compromised or suspected to be.
Enforce strong authentication everywhere and strictly control privileged accounts.
Harden access filtering to prevent data exfiltration.
Strengthen security of internet-exposed applications and those linked to third-party networks.
Notify affected people where the nature of the data requires it.

summary: CERT-FR's second REACTIV situation report counts 64 new data violations since September 30, five of them at ministries or their agencies: a foreign ministry library portal, the OFB permit portal, France Travail (over 60,000 agents and professionals), CAF's VACAF (about 1.2 million case files) and the ASP DEFI portal (30,500 users). ANSSI found no new weakness types: missing multi-factor sign-in, infostealer-stolen accounts, supplier exposure and IDOR flaws recur.

action: Install Check Point's November Jumbo Hotfix on all Management Servers and Security Gateways, starting with internet-facing Mobile Access deployments. Hunt for the published indicators and ask Check Point Support for an exposure assessment.
exec: A fix existed a week before the attacks; only unpatched gateways were hit, and a small number in one region were wiped.
plain: Check Point says attackers broke into about two dozen of its security devices that lacked a fix issued on October 23. Some Israeli organisations had data wiped; later attacks in other countries were not destructive.

key_findings: Attackers used PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619, CVSS 9.2) in the Mobile Access Portal for unauthenticated code execution, then CVE-2026-123039 to become root.
Exploitation began October 30, about a week after the PHP2Shell hotfix of October 23; the advisory counts a couple of dozen compromised unpatched systems.
The first wave targeted Israeli organisations and was destructive in a limited number of cases; a second wave from November 2 reached organisations in several countries with no destruction reported.
Tools included the TSGA backdoor, a TSProxy library, PHP webshells, a network scanner and a wiper that was also run on a VMware ESXi host reached over SSH.
Check Point Research links the tooling to the PhiliKit framework but does not attribute the campaign with confidence and raises a possible false flag.

recommendations: Install the November Jumbo Hotfix on all Management Servers and Security Gateways as soon as possible.

Contact Check Point Support for exposure assessment; absence of an indicator match does not rule out compromise.

title: Elastic: SANSAR Linux cryptominer fakes GPU readings to hide mining
actor: REF3364 (Elastic's tracking name; financially motivated, unattributed)
summary: Elastic Security Labs describes REF3364, a Linux cryptomining operation seen in late October 2026. Access came through an exposed Ray job agent. The toolkit, SANSAR, adds a kernel rootkit, a modified NVIDIA NVML wrapper that reports 0% GPU use and random temperatures, and an Ethereum-assisted backdoor. Elastic does not identify who is behind it.
plain: Attackers are secretly mining cryptocurrency on Linux servers with powerful graphics cards, and they fake the card's readings so the load looks normal.
exec: Hijacked AI compute raises costs and takes capacity from real workloads, and fake monitoring readings hide it.
action: Do not expose Ray job APIs to the internet, restrict who can submit jobs, and check hosts for a modified NVML library, unknown DKMS modules such as acpi_thermal_mgr and initramfs changes.

key_findings: Organisations running Linux GPU hosts for AI or ML work are the target; three hosts were hit in an intrusion tracked as REF3364 between 22 and 25 October 2026.
Initial access was an internet-reachable Ray job agent that accepted job submissions without authentication, followed by a reverse shell and an added SSH key.
The Rust orchestrator SANSAR takes commands over Tor, runs XMRig and SRBMiner-MULTI for mining, and can open shells and run a TCP SYN flood task.
A kernel rootkit (acpi_thermal_mgr.ko) hides selected processes, files and sockets, and a modified NVML library reports 0% GPU use with random temperature and power readings.
A separate netns backdoor gets its controller address from an Ethereum contract through public RPC and opens a shell on port 8080.
recommendations: Check who can submit jobs to GPU clusters and do not leave job agents such as Ray reachable without authentication.
Check whether GPU monitoring libraries such as NVML have been modified.

action: Join calls through the official Zoom or Teams app with an invite code, keep the webcam off until the host is verified another way, never run scripts or paste code to fix audio, and enable MFA and login alerts on messaging accounts.
exec: A trusted contact on a video call can be a recording; crypto firms and open-source maintainers are the targets, with supply-chain risk for software users.
plain: The FBI says North Korean hackers stage fake video meetings using real recordings of earlier victims, then trick people into running a so-called fix that infects their computer and empties crypto wallets.

key_findings: Targets are cryptocurrency and Web3 workers, open-source developers and maintainers, and through them their contacts and employers' networks.
Operators take over a victim's messaging account, send contacts a look-alike meeting link and replay the victim's recorded webcam video in a staged session.
Posing as the contact, they claim an audio fault and have the target run an update or paste terminal code, installing a backdoor, keyloggers and a cookie harvester.
More than $400 million was stolen over roughly 18 months and the FBI seized over 900 victim webcam videos; one widely used JavaScript library was nearly compromised.
New elements are AI-generated deepfakes of known crypto figures, attempts on NPM and Rust maintainers, and theft delayed for months after compromise.
recommendations: Join meetings through the official Zoom or Teams app with an invite code rather than a web link.
Keep your camera off until you have verified the inviter, and confirm meetings through a different channel.
Never run scripts or paste code into a terminal to fix a meeting problem.
Enable multifactor authentication and login alerts on messaging accounts.
If compromised, move crypto to a new wallet with new seed phrases on a clean device and report to IC3 with the keyword FaceStealer.

summary: FBI FLASH AC-111226-MS (TLP:CLEAR) attributes the FaceStealer scheme to North Korean state-sponsored hackers (Sapphire Sleet, UNC1069, BlueNoroff). They hijack a victim's messaging account, invite contacts to a counterfeit Zoom or Teams call, replay recorded webcam video and push a fake audio fix that installs malware. The FBI says over $400 million was stolen in about 18 months.

action: Search your GitHub organisations for wfx-docs branches and pull requests titled 'docs: dependency audit notes', and look for gaps in workflow run numbers. Where the payload ran, rotate every secret and cloud role those workflows could reach.
exec: Hijacked developer accounts are being used to plant key-stealing code in software projects, a risk for any team building on GitHub.
plain: Attackers used 4,837 taken-over GitHub accounts to probe more than 61,000 code projects and ran password-stealing code in the build systems of at least 1,835 of them.

key_findings: From about 12:45 UTC on November 10, 4,837 compromised GitHub accounts opened probe pull requests in 61,764 repositories to test for write access.
At least 1,835 repositories ran the payload and had credentials taken; the true figure may be higher because run logs were deleted.
The stealer arrives through an altered workflow, an npm postinstall hook or a throwaway workflow, and is reverted within about a minute.
It takes Actions secrets, cloud and registry credentials and AI provider keys, then pivots into AWS, GCP, Azure, Vault and Kubernetes.
New tricks include forged success status checks, rewritten AWS role trust policies and Azure federated credentials named wfx-ci for persistence.
recommendations: Search for wfx-docs branches and pull requests titled 'docs: dependency audit notes'.
Check for gaps in workflow run numbers, which may be the only trace of a run.
If the payload ran, rotate every secret and cloud role available to that repository's workflows.
Review AWS role trust policies and remove Azure federated credentials named wfx-ci.
Treat machines that installed the affected Packagist or Go module versions as compromised.

summary: Aikido reports that from November 10 an attacker used 4,837 compromised GitHub accounts to open probe pull requests in 61,764 repositories, then ran a secrets-stealing script in the build pipelines of at least 1,835. The script takes pipeline secrets and cloud credentials, pivots into cloud accounts and erases its traces within about a minute. One Packagist package and two Go module versions also carried it.
title: wfx-loot campaign uses 4,837 hijacked GitHub accounts to push secrets-stealing malware

action: Follow Unit 42's guidance: tighten identity hygiene (strong unique passwords, no shared or default credentials), cut internet-facing attack surface, patch dated public flaws, and add the two published IP indicators to monitoring.
exec: AI-run intrusions got in through weak passwords, open cloud storage and login bypasses, not new exploits; basic identity and patch upkeep is the defence.
plain: Unit 42 says a likely China-linked group used an AI hacking tool to run 25 mostly automated break-in attempts on 19 chip, defence and civil-society bodies, got into 10 and took over 1 million union member records.

key_findings: Targets were 7 semiconductor and advanced-manufacturing firms, 3 defence or defence-policy bodies and 4 human-rights or civil-society groups, including a Canadian rights body and a US teachers' union.
The cluster ran 25 operations against at least 19 organisations and reached confirmed unauthorised access or data retrieval at 10 of them.
It used a customised fork of the open-source Cairn framework driven by Zhipu GLM 5.2 and DeepSeek V4 models, plus a custom skill pack not in upstream Cairn.
Entry came from password spraying, brute-forced credentials, unauthenticated cloud-storage writes, login bypasses and open registration endpoints rather than new exploits.
Data taken included over 1 million union member records, about 31,000 CRM contacts and about 150,000 internal documents; Unit 42 assesses China-nexus collection with moderate confidence.
recommendations: Tighten identity hygiene: remove weak, default and shared passwords on internet-facing applications.
Reduce the exposed attack surface, including open registration endpoints and unauthenticated cloud storage.
Patch software affected by older public CVEs.
Monitor for the two IP addresses Unit 42 published for the Cairn hosting and staging servers.

summary: Unit 42 tracked a cluster, CL-STA-1238, running a customised fork of the open-source Cairn AI penetration-testing framework on Chinese AI models. It ran 25 operations against at least 19 organisations in the semiconductor supply chain, defence and civil society, with confirmed access or data retrieval at 10. action: Barracuda Managed XDR Cloud or Monitored Endpoint customers who were contacted: revoke and recreate API integration credentials. Everyone: retire long-lived keys held by third parties, use short-lived scoped credentials, and rehearse rotating secrets at scale.

key_findings: The attacker used a cloud access key Barracuda had issued to a third-party AI vendor for a past project and never retired; the vendor's development environment was compromised in October.
Activity ran from November 1 04:33 UTC to November 2 23:31 UTC and touched about 10 cloud accounts; it was noticed on November 4 after it had stopped.

Barracuda attributes the method, not the actor, to the open-source ARTEX AI penetration-testing framework.
recommendations: Remove standing credentials, especially long-lived keys held by third parties; use short-lived, narrowly scoped ones.
Limit blast radius so no single credential opens the next system.
Assume compromise and be able to rotate secrets at scale and rebuild from known-good states.
Customers contacted by Barracuda should revoke and recreate Managed XDR API integration credentials.

action: Mobile operators: deploy GTP-C and GTP-U security aligned with SS7 and Diameter firewalls, treat the IPX interface as untrusted, and monitor internal signalling, not only the edge. High-risk users: avoid SMS login codes.
exec: Phone networks themselves were compromised, so calls and SMS codes can be intercepted without touching the handset.
plain: Telecom security firm Enea says one hacking group took over parts of Asian phone networks to intercept calls and texts, mostly of people in Taiwan, while a second group hid spying tools inside operators' data links.

key_findings: SilentAir ran attacks from compromised SS7 and Diameter nodes inside operators in at least six Asian countries, reaching a dozen more countries with Taiwan the main target.
It redirects subscribers' location registration to intercept calls and SMS, with one-time codes seen arriving right after interception; some targets were political and government VIPs.
Enea assesses with high confidence that SilentAir is a state-level actor and, at low confidence, China-aligned; it works a UTC+8 pattern and avoids Chinese networks.
LIMINAL PANDA uses GTPDoor implants, including a new variant hiding commands in GTP-U traffic, for covert control and exfiltration tunnels between infected operators.
Enea saw several hundred covert command attempts since Q1 2026 and at least 5 to 10 infected operators, possibly several dozen worldwide.
recommendations: Deploy GTP-C and GTP-U security and align it with SS7 and Diameter firewalls for cross-protocol visibility.
Treat the IPX interface as untrusted and inspect all traffic more deeply.
Monitor internal signalling protocols and tools, not just the network edge.
Integrate signalling security with IT security and reconsider outsourcing of core networks.

summary: Enea describes two actors inside mobile networks. SilentAir, assessed as state-level, used compromised SS7 and Diameter nodes in at least six Asian countries to redirect and intercept calls and texts, mainly of Taiwanese subscribers, including one-time codes. LIMINAL PANDA used GTPDoor implants for covert command traffic and data theft between operators; Enea saw at least 5 to 10 infected operators. A link between the two is unconfirmed.
title: SilentAir and LIMINAL PANDA exploit mobile networks to spy on subscribers

validation.note: Reviewed against the original Enea report.

review.note: Compared with Enea report: six Asian countries, Taiwan, high/low confidence, GTPDoor, 5-10 operators, link unconfirmed; summary names Enea as attributing

action: Schools and universities: check whether your accounts appear in stolen-credential data, reset those passwords through a trusted process, revoke sessions, review mailbox rules and turn on phishing-resistant sign-in. Monitor outbound mail for bulk sending.
exec: Stolen staff or student logins can be reused to send threats under an institution's name, causing disruption and reputational harm.
plain: Schools across Europe received threatening emails on November 11. Researchers found that two university email addresses reported as senders, in Egypt and Taiwan, had already appeared in stolen-password data.

key_findings: Hudson Rock found two university addresses reported as senders of the threats, one Egyptian and one Taiwanese, in previously stolen credential data.
The Egyptian address sits in a Vidar infostealer record dated October 1, 2021, with 112 saved credentials, 20 of them using that address.
The Taiwanese address appears in the AlienTXTBASE collection, more than a year old; the university later saw abnormal bulk sending and suspended the account.
About 6,000 Italian schools received the messages, more than 300 in Northern Ireland, with threats also reported in Scotland and Ireland.
Hudson Rock says this shows earlier exposure, not proof the credentials were used, and attributes the threats to no person, group or state.
recommendations: Contain any affected account and reset its credentials through a trusted process.
Revoke sessions and refresh tokens and review app passwords, sign-in methods, app consents and mailbox rules.
Investigate and clean the infected device.
Move to phishing-resistant sign-in and monitor outbound mail for bulk sending.
Use leaked-credential detection and risk-based access policies.

summary: Threat emails reached about 6,000 Italian schools (per ANSA, citing the Education Ministry) and more than 300 in Northern Ireland (PSNI) on November 11; threats were also reported in Scotland and Ireland. Hudson Rock found two university addresses reported as senders, one Egyptian and one Taiwanese, in infostealer data that predates the threats by a year or more. It stresses this shows earlier credential exposure, not proof of use, and names no culprit.
title: School bomb-threat emails across Europe traced to accounts found in infostealer data

validation.note: Reviewed against the original Hudson Rock report.

review.note: Summary said hundreds of schools in NI, Scotland, Ireland; sources give 300+ for NI only (PSNI), no counts elsewhere; fixed and added correction file. Other facts match Hudson Rock and Security Affairs

action: Check your email address on Have I Been Pwned. If it appears, change that password everywhere it was reused and turn on two-step sign-in.

Only about 107,000 belonged to forum members; the rest were victims' credentials that members had posted. The same day it added a 2023 breach of Sberbank's SberSpasibo loyalty programme with 3.3 million unique emails.

action: After any web server compromise, remove the GSocket client, its persistence and staged files, then confirm relay connections have stopped. Apply deny-by-default outbound rules and audit cron entries, systemd units and shell startup files.
attack: T1059.004 Command and Scripting Interpreter: Unix Shell
exec: Patching a hacked web server is not enough; a relay tool left behind keeps attackers in, and it has no fixed address to block.
plain: Microsoft warns that hackers who break into Linux web servers are leaving behind a free relay tool that keeps them connected even after the original hole is fixed.

key_findings: Internet-facing Linux web servers are the target; Among web-application and hosting incidents, PHP applications and cPanel hosting account for 63.9% and Apache for 24.3%.
Education and research is the most affected sector at 30.7% of organisations, which Microsoft attributes to exposure rather than deliberate targeting.
After web application code execution, a curl download-and-run script installs GSocket, which connects outbound to a shared public relay.
Access persists after the original flaw is patched, and there is no attacker-owned address or domain to block.
Devices with GSocket detections rose 356.2% from March to August 2026; in few observed incidents attackers also tried the Dirty Frag flaw CVE-2026-43284 to gain root.
recommendations: Remediate the host, not just the vulnerability: remove the GSocket client, persistence and staged files and confirm relay connections stop.
Apply deny-by-default egress rules and monitor connections to relay infrastructure.
Mount temporary and memory-backed directories as non-executable and alert on execution from hidden or world-writable paths.
Audit cron entries, systemd units and shell startup files.
Hunt for gs-netcat or gsocket processes and staging files under /dev/shm.

summary: Microsoft says multiple unrelated attackers are installing the open-source GSocket tool on Linux web servers after exploiting web applications. Both the server and the attacker connect outbound to a shared public relay, so there is no attacker address to block and access survives patching of the original flaw. Devices with GSocket detections rose 356.2% between March and August 2026, with PHP and cPanel hosting most affected.
title: Microsoft: attackers use open-source GSocket to keep hidden access to hacked Linux servers

validation.note: Reviewed against the original Microsoft Threat Intelligence report.

review.note: Checked against Microsoft post: 63.9%/24.3% are shares within web-app/hosting incidents and 356.2% is devices with detections, Dirty Frag only in few incidents; wording fixed

action: Apply Fortinet's updates to FortiOS, FortiManager, FortiAnalyzer, FortiSASE, FortiPAM and FortiSandbox after testing, and administer them from segmented systems that are not internet-connected.
exec: A large Fortinet patch batch with no known exploitation; plan prompt but orderly updates, starting with management consoles.
plain: Fortinet released fixes for dozens of flaws in its firewall and management products. No attacks are known yet, but the worst could let an intruder take control.

key_findings: Affected products include FortiOS 8.0.0-8.0.1 and 7.6.0-7.6.7, FortiManager and FortiAnalyzer 8.0.0-8.0.2, FortiSASE, FortiPAM and FortiSandbox, plus older branches.
The advisory lists 46 CVEs, 37 of them in FortiManager and FortiAnalyzer.
The most severe flaws could allow arbitrary code execution, with impact depending on the privileges of the affected account.
No exploitation in the wild had been reported at publication.
Risk is rated High for government and business entities of every size and Low for home users.
recommendations: Apply Fortinet's updates to vulnerable systems immediately after appropriate testing.
Keep network infrastructure on current, supported software and remediate detected vulnerabilities at least monthly.
Apply least privilege and disable or secure default accounts.
Use dedicated, segmented, non-internet-connected systems for administrative work.

action: Identify Linux systems running OpenSSH before 10.6p2 on musl libc without PAM that accept password logins, and update to 10.6p2. Until then, disable password authentication or turn SSH off on those systems.
exec: The flaw applies only to a narrow combination of settings, but where all four conditions hold the result may be root access.
plain: New Zealand's cyber agency warned of a flaw in OpenSSH, the standard tool for logging in to Linux machines remotely, that could let an attacker in as the top-level user on certain lightweight Linux systems.

key_findings: CVE-2026-123158, also called SSHole, is an authentication bypass in OpenSSH on Linux that may allow root access.
All four conditions must hold: version earlier than 10.6p2, musl libc, no Pluggable Authentication Modules, and password logins accepted.
OpenSSH 10.6p2 fixes the flaw.
The alert gives no CVSS score and does not say whether the flaw is being exploited.
recommendations: Update to OpenSSH 10.6p2.
As mitigation, disable password authentication or disable SSH.
Identify potentially affected systems in your environment.
Apply vendor patches or mitigations as they become available and follow the OpenSSH release notes.

summary: New Zealand's NCSC issued an alert on November 11 about CVE-2026-123158, nicknamed SSHole, an authentication bypass in OpenSSH on Linux that may give an attacker root access. A system is exposed only if it runs a version before 10.6p2, uses musl libc, does not use PAM and accepts password logins. The alert does not say whether the flaw is being exploited.
title: NCSC New Zealand alerts on OpenSSH 'SSHole' authentication bypass CVE-2026-123158

review.note: Compared title, Nov 11 date, four conditions, 10.6p2 fix, mitigation and no-exploitation statement against the NCSC NZ alert; KEV listing in cve_meta not claimed in text

action: UK critical infrastructure, government and larger organisations: use the NCSC's Find a Provider page to choose an assured CyAS supplier, and consider adversary simulation alongside the Cyber Assessment Framework and Cyber Resilience Audit.
exec: UK critical-sector bodies get an assured route to adversary-simulation testing; regulators may use it as common evidence.
plain: Britain's cyber agency started a scheme that vets companies offering realistic mock attacks, so important organisations can choose a trusted firm to test their defences.

key_findings: The NCSC launched the Cyber Adversary Simulation (CyAS) scheme, which assures suppliers of adversary simulation services against an NCSC-defined standard.
It is aimed at the UK's most critical organisations and their Cyber Oversight Bodies, with larger organisations, critical national infrastructure and government highlighted.
Providers do reconnaissance, build customer-specific attack plans and pursue agreed objectives without being limited to purchased threat intelligence or documented techniques.
CyAS complements the Cyber Assessment Framework and the Cyber Resilience Audit scheme and was developed with regulators and lead government departments.
The scheme launches as a minimum viable product so the NCSC can test demand and refine the method; the release names no providers.
recommendations: Use the scheme's Find a Provider page to identify assured adversary simulation providers.
Consider CyAS alongside the Cyber Assessment Framework and Cyber Resilience Audit to build a fuller picture of security and resilience.

summary: The UK's NCSC launched the Cyber Adversary Simulation (CyAS) scheme on November 11. It assesses commercial suppliers against an NCSC standard so that critical organisations, government and their oversight bodies can pick trusted providers to run realistic simulated attacks. It sits alongside the Cyber Assessment Framework and Cyber Resilience Audit scheme and starts as a minimum viable product while demand and method are tested.
title: NCSC (UK) launches Cyber Adversary Simulation scheme to assure attack-simulation providers

title: CloudSEK: Silent Lynx group took Tajik government documents, including Defence Ministry mail, via railway employee account
date_note: Date of CloudSEK's report as relayed by BES.media on 12 November; the activity ran from mid-August to at least 10 October 2026.
summary: Per a Reuters report relayed by BES.media, security firm CloudSEK attributes the intrusion to the Silent Lynx group, which entered Tajikistan's government e-document system through a Tajik railway employee's account, from mid-August to at least 10 October. plain: Researchers say a hacking group read Tajikistan's government document system for about two months and copied thousands of documents, including defence mail. Governments have not confirmed it.

action: Review browser extensions installed in developer mode, especially utilities asking for broad permissions. Audit webmail and case-management pages for script tags loading from unfamiliar domains, and investigate OneDrive activity to tenants outside your organisation.
exec: Browser-based spying leaves few traces on disk, so endpoint tools can miss it; webmail portals and browser extensions need checking.
plain: Researchers found spies running hidden code inside the web browsers of government workers in the Middle East and Southeast Asia, stealing logins and reading email without leaving files on the computer.

key_findings: Targets were defence, interior and foreign ministries, a telecom provider and government email in the Middle East, plus police, justice, military and foreign affairs bodies in Southeast Asia.
Falcon C2 runs JavaScript in the victim's browser over encrypted WebSockets to steal passwords, cookies and email and to proxy through logged-in sessions.
Entry methods were script tags injected into a ministry's Roundcube webmail (39 instances affected), a fake Flash update and a sideloaded 'PDF Viewer' extension requesting 40 permissions.
A Rust implant named Antino uses Microsoft OneDrive as its command channel.
Unit 42 assesses with high confidence that Falcon and the earlier PeckBirdy framework are variants of one core; it names no actor.
recommendations: Review extensions installed in developer mode that pose as utilities and request permissions such as all URLs, debugger or native messaging.
Audit webmail, ticketing and case-management pages for script tags loading from unfamiliar external domains.
Look for web-analytics style cookies or storage keys on internal apps where analytics has no reason to appear.
Investigate OAuth activity to OneDrive tenants outside your organisation, especially repeated small JSON writes.

summary: Unit 42 reports that a framework called Falcon C2 ran malicious JavaScript inside the browsers of government staff in one Middle Eastern and four Southeast Asian countries between March and May 2026. It steals passwords, cookies and email, and lets attackers browse as the victim. Delivery included injected scripts on a foreign ministry's Roundcube webmail and a fake PDF viewer extension. No actor is named.
title: Unit 42: Falcon C2 turns victims' browsers into spying tools at Middle East and Asian ministries

validation.note: Reviewed against the original Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 report.

review.note: Unit 42 Nov 11: 1 Middle East + 4 SE Asian countries, Mar-May 2026, Roundcube on foreign ministry, fake PDF extension, no actor named match.

action: Government, telecom and critical infrastructure security teams: load Check Point's published indicators, hunt for the listed registry and firewall artifacts, and warn staff that a browser certificate error offering a fix installer is a lure.
actor: CopperDragon (tool developer for China-nexus groups, moderate confidence)
exec: Shared tooling across China-linked espionage groups means a detection for one campaign may help against the others.
plain: Check Point found that three separate spying campaigns in Europe, Asia and Latin America used related malicious software from one developer, which appears to supply several China-linked hacking groups.

key_findings: Check Point tracks the builder of the Sparrow framework as CopperDragon, a possible tool supplier to China-nexus groups including FamousSparrow, Earth Estries and Tropic Trooper; confidence is moderate.
SilentDelivery hit government, shipping and IT targets in Europe and Asia from early 2026 using watering-hole sites with a fake Chrome certificate error and a bogus fix installer.
OceanGate targeted government and critical infrastructure in Asia through an internet-facing Linux server, then RDP password attempts against Windows administrators.
DarkWire has targeted telecom providers and foreign affairs and justice ministries in Latin America since mid-2025; its link to the group is weaker.
New tools include SquadC, AnnobinDoor, SparrowShell with an embedded Linux kernel rootkit, CopperDNS, and a passive backdoor hiding on a legitimate port.
recommendations: Hunt for the host artifacts Check Point lists, including a WindowsUpdateAssist Run key and firewall rules named RasiUwpApp and ss1.
Check for an unexpected LocalAccountTokenFilterPolicy change and an account named admin$.
Load the published hashes, domains, addresses and certificate details into detection.

summary: Check Point Research links three espionage campaigns through the Sparrow malware framework, whose builder it tracks as CopperDragon, a possible tool supplier to several China-nexus groups. SilentDelivery used watering-hole sites in Europe and Asia, OceanGate hit government and critical infrastructure in Asia through Linux servers, and DarkWire targeted Latin American telecoms and ministries. Several backdoors and a Linux kernel rootkit are newly documented.
title: Three China-nexus espionage campaigns linked through Sparrow malware ecosystem

attack: T1114.002 Email Collection: Remote Email Collection
exec: The malware never calls out; it lives inside the Exchange server and blends with normal mail traffic, so network monitoring alone will not catch it.
plain: ESET found new spying tools from the Russia-aligned Turla group on government email servers in Kazakhstan and Romania. The tools hide inside the mail server and copy messages exchanged with NATO and EU bodies.

key_findings: ESET attributes the Cereal toolset to Turla (Snake) with high confidence, citing concurrent use of a known Turla component and similarity to older Turla malware.
Victims are two national government organisations: Kazakhstan (found November 28, 2025) and Romania (compromised December 23, 2025).
CerealNeuron is a passive backdoor that listens for web requests on Exchange-like paths, so there is no outbound command traffic to spot.
CerealBox is injected into the Exchange transport process and wraps transport agent handlers to stage mail; in Romania it collected messages involving NATO and EU addresses.
The post does not say how the attackers first got in; fuller analysis is in a separate ESET white paper.
recommendations: Check Exchange servers against the indicators ESET publishes in its malware-ioc GitHub repository.
Do not rely on network detection: the traffic uses OWA, Autodiscover and ActiveSync paths and blends with legitimate Exchange traffic.

summary: ESET Research attributes, with high confidence, a previously unknown toolset called Cereal to Russia-aligned Turla. It was found on Exchange servers of two national government bodies: in Kazakhstan on November 28, 2025 and in Romania, compromised December 23, 2025. A passive backdoor listens on Exchange-like web paths, and a collector injected into the mail transport process staged messages involving NATO and EU addresses. Initial access is not described.
title: Turla uses new Cereal toolset to steal email from government Exchange servers

plain: A researcher published an unfixed Windows flaw, named SignDrop, that lets someone who already has basic access to a computer gain full control of it by misusing built-in protections. No fix exists yet.

key_findings: A researcher using the name MSNightmare (Nightmare-Eclipse cluster) published SignDrop on GitHub on November 10, 2026 without coordinated disclosure.

It raises a standard user to SYSTEM without memory corruption, abusing CLFS HMAC authentication and the Defender signature-update RPC interface to plant a file, then sideloading a DLL through consent.exe.
Cyderes reproduced all five stages and got a SYSTEM shell with no UAC prompt; the exploit deletes its planted DLL afterwards.
No CVE or patch exists; Microsoft had not commented as of November 11 and no in-the-wild use was identified as of November 10.
It is the cluster's sixteenth public zero-day in about thirty-one weeks; the researcher's claim that about 80% of installations are vulnerable is unsupported.
recommendations: Inventory the CLFS Authentication Mode registry value across hosts to define which systems to prioritise.
Do not disable CLFS authentication, because that reopens older memory-corruption attack classes.
Restrict untrusted local code execution with application and script control.
Deploy the detections Cyderes lists, such as Defender signature-update RPC calls from outside the Defender service tree and any hid.dll created in the ink directory.
Retain file-creation and image-load telemetry, since the exploit removes its artifact.

summary: A researcher using the name MSNightmare published SignDrop on November 10, an unpatched Windows flaw that lifts a standard user to SYSTEM by abusing CLFS log authentication and Microsoft Defender's signature-update interface. Cyderes reproduced it in a controlled environment and got a SYSTEM shell. There is no CVE or patch; as of November 11 Microsoft had not commented, and no use in real attacks had been confirmed.
title: SignDrop: researcher releases Windows zero-day giving SYSTEM privileges

validation.note: Reviewed against the original Cyderes Howler Cell document. Microsoft has published nothing on this flaw that could be found.

review.note: Removed unsupported Nov 12 reproduction date; Microsoft no-comment as of Nov 11

action: Update Google Chrome to 157.0.8103.50 or later and relaunch the browser; do not wait for the staged rollout. IT teams: push the update to managed devices and check that other Chromium-based browsers have their equivalent fix.
exec: An actively exploited browser flaw affects nearly every organisation; updating is quick and low-cost.
plain: Google released a Chrome browser update that fixes nine security flaws, including one that attackers were already using against people.

key_findings: Chrome stable moved to 157.0.8103.50/.51 on Windows and Mac and 157.0.8103.50 on Linux, with nine security fixes.
Google says it is aware that an exploit for CVE-2026-125350, a high-severity use-after-free in XML, exists in the wild.
Other high-severity fixes cover WebGL, FileSystem, Compositing, GPU and a V8 type confusion (CVE-2026-125344).
The exploited bug was reported by an outside researcher on October 12 and again anonymously on November 6.
Rollout is staged over days and weeks, and bug details stay restricted until most users are updated.
recommendations: Update Chrome to 157.0.8103.50/.51 (Windows, Mac) or 157.0.8103.50 (Linux) and relaunch.
Do not wait for the staged rollout; trigger the update manually or push it to managed devices.

title: Chrome 157 fixes eighth exploited zero-day of 2026

action: No action needed; for awareness. Organisations holding Washington residents' data: breaches affecting more than 500 residents must be reported to the Attorney General's Office.
date_note: Date of the Attorney General's news release; Insurance Journal covered the report on 19 November.
exec: Cyberattacks, with ransomware the most common method, were the leading cause of reported breaches in Washington state.
plain: Washington's attorney general reports 197 data breaches over one year, with more than 3.5 million notices sent to residents. Cyberattacks were the leading cause, and ransomware was the most common method.

key_findings: 197 data breaches were reported to the Washington AG's Office between July 24, 2025 and July 23, 2026, with more than 3.5 million notices sent to residents.
Cyberattacks were the leading cause with 139 incidents; ransomware was the most common method, responsible for 86 incidents.
Social Security numbers were exposed in 148 breaches, which the release describes as over 75% of all reported breaches.
No breach affecting 1 million or more Washington residents was reported, and both breach and notice counts declined from the previous reporting year.
recommendations: Expand the legal definition of personal information to include ITINs, Tribal identification and enrollment numbers, IRS Identity Protection PINs, precise geolocation data, and the last four digits of Social Security numbers combined with a name.
Require entities that own or license Washingtonians' personal information to maintain reasonable security procedures.
Require notification when an AI agent operated by an entity gains unauthorized access to a Washington resident's personal information.

action: Take SSH off the internet and require two-factor sign-in for remote access. Patch VMware vCenter and anything still exposed to Log4Shell. Software makers: isolate signing servers and review their logs for unexpected use.
exec: Attackers were positioned for a supply-chain attack on a developer's customers; the signing step was blocked, but only just.
plain: Kaspersky found that a hacking group spent months inside a Russian software company and tried to tamper with the server that digitally signs its software. Security software blocked that attempt.

key_findings: The victim is a Russia-based developer of industrial software used mainly in Eastern Europe; Kaspersky attributes the intrusion to BO Team (Black Owl) with high confidence.
Entry was through internet-exposed SSH on a Linux terminal server with a password-authenticated service account; Log4Shell in vCenter 7.0.3 then gave root on a hypervisor.
Attackers stayed for several months and reached domain controllers, GitLab, the Ansible server, backups, SIEM and the mail server, stealing its DKIM private key.
Attempts to inject code on the code-signing server were blocked by security software; no signed malware distribution, encryption or destruction is reported.
The stolen DKIM key let them send phishing that passed sender checks, and they mostly lived off the land rather than deploying malware.
recommendations: Remove internet exposure of SSH, disable root SSH login and require two-factor sign-in for VPN, RDP and domain controllers.
Patch vCenter, hypervisors and any software still affected by Log4j.
After an intrusion reset all account passwords, reset krbtgt twice and reissue keys and certificates.
Keep backups on a non-domain server with separate credentials and test restores.
Keep logs at least 30 days and remove plaintext credentials from scripts and directory comments.

summary: Kaspersky ICS CERT describes a months-long intrusion at a Russian industrial software developer, attributed with high confidence to BO Team. The attackers entered through internet-exposed SSH, used Log4Shell in VMware vCenter to gain root on a hypervisor, and reached domain controllers, GitLab and the mail server. Their attempts to inject code on the code-signing server were blocked, and no tampered software release is reported.
title: BO Team spends months inside a Russian software developer, targets its build-signing server
